questions.q: Tell me about yourself.
questions.tests: Whether you can tell, in 90 seconds, a coherent story that leads naturally to this role, and how you communicate: concision, energy, priorities. It is the first impression and often shapes the questions that follow.
structure: Open with the present: current role and one concrete achievement (Present, 20-25 seconds)
Link to the past: 2-3 steps that built the relevant skills, for example university and your first experiences in finance (Past, 30-35 seconds)
Make the common thread explicit: what led you to M&A and the tech sector
Close with the future: why this programme and this bank, now (Future, 20-25 seconds)
good: An explicit common thread (e.g. an interest in technology and transactions) that connects every step
At least one concrete fact: a grade, a number of deals, the size of a transaction
A length of 75-90 seconds and an ending that invites the next question
pitfalls: Repeating your CV line by line in chronological order
Starting from secondary school or from irrelevant personal details
Closing without linking the story to the role you are applying for
questions.skeleton: I'm currently an analyst at [boutique], an M&A advisory firm focused on [semiconductors and deep tech], where I have worked on [number] live mandates, most recently [type of deal]. I got here through [your MSc], where I graduated [with top marks] and focused on [area]. What connects these steps is [your common thread, e.g. how technology reshapes industries and how transactions finance that change]. I am now applying to [programme] because I want [larger deals, broader product exposure, an international platform], and [Bank] is where [specific reason].

steps: Time yourself: if you go over 2 minutes you are listing, not telling a story; cut the steps that do not lead to the role.
Reread your first sentence: it must say who you are today and what you do, with a concrete fact, not where you were born.
Check the final bridge: the last sentence must explain why this programme is the logical next step.
explanation.shortcut: Present, Past, Future: three blocks, one common thread, 90 seconds.
explanation.trap: Turning the answer into a reading of your CV: the interviewer already has it in front of them and is looking for the logic behind your choices, not the list.
explanation.rule: Every step you mention must help explain why you are here today.

questions.q: Why investment banking?
questions.tests: Whether your motivation is genuine and informed: whether you know what a banker really does and whether you already have evidence that you chose this job knowing its costs.
structure: Open with the main reason in one sentence (e.g. working on decisions that change a company's trajectory)
Proof 1: a concrete experience in which you did the work and enjoyed it (models, M&A processes at a boutique)
Proof 2: what attracts you to the role specifically: learning curve, exposure to clients and senior bankers, variety of sectors
Close by linking to where you want to grow: execution of larger and cross-border deals
good: Reasons tied to the content of the work, not to salary or prestige
Examples from your boutique experience: you have already seen the work from the inside
Awareness of the sacrifices, stated naturally and without drama
pitfalls: Generic answers such as 'I love finance' or 'it is fast-paced and challenging' with no proof
Citing money, status or exit opportunities as the main motivation
Describing the job incorrectly, for example as 'investing in companies'
questions.skeleton: I want to work in investment banking because I enjoy being close to the decisions that change a company's trajectory, such as [a sale, an acquisition, a capital raise]. I have tested this at [boutique]: on [deal], I [built the model / drafted the information memorandum / ran the buyer list], and what I enjoyed most was [specific element]. Banking also gives me the steepest learning curve I know of: in [timeframe] I learned [skill]. I want to keep building that on [larger, cross-border transactions], which is why I am applying for this role.

steps: Check that there is at least one lived proof: a deal, a model, a specific task, not just adjectives.
Make sure the motivation is about the work (analysis, transactions, clients) and not the benefits (money, exits to PE).
Remove every sentence that would also apply to consulting or private equity: what remains must be specific to banking.
explanation.shortcut: One reason, two proofs from your experience, one link to the future.
explanation.trap: Talking about a 'dynamic and challenging environment': everyone says it and it proves nothing.
explanation.rule: Motivation is demonstrated by what you have already done, not by what you say you feel.

questions.q: Why do you want to join our bank rather than one of our competitors?
questions.tests: Whether you have done real research and whether your choice is reasoned. The interviewer is looking for specific reasons that would not apply to a competitor bank.
structure: Open with a summary: 'Three reasons: the business, the people and the programme'
Business: a concrete strength of the bank that is relevant to you, with verifiable proof (a recent deal, a league-table position, a figure from the annual report)
People: what you learned from talking to those who work there, citing the context (event, coffee chat) without naming names
Programme: what it concretely offers you (rotations, training, mobility, type of clients)
Close by linking the three reasons to your profile and your goals
good: It passes the genericity test: if you swap the bank's name, the answer no longer holds
Tailor the business point to the bank: for example the international network for HSBC, global scale for J.P. Morgan, the London-New York axis for Barclays
Link at least one reason to your experience in tech and semiconductors
pitfalls: Generic praise such as 'leading global bank' or 'great culture'
Citing wrong or out-of-date figures about the bank
Criticising competitors to make the bank look better
questions.skeleton: Three reasons. First, [Bank]'s strength in [sector, region or product], which I saw in [recent deal or league-table position]; that is exactly the type of work I want to do after [my experience at boutique]. Second, the people: at [event or conversation], [analysts from the team] described [specific aspect of the culture, e.g. early responsibility], which matches how I work best. Third, the programme itself: [rotation, training, international mobility] would give me [specific skill or exposure]. Together, these make [Bank] the place where I can [career goal].

steps: Run the genericity test: mentally replace the bank's name with a competitor's; every sentence that still holds true must be rewritten.
Check that every reason has a proof: a deal, a number, a conversation.
Make sure at least one reason is about you: why that strength matters for your path.
explanation.shortcut: Business, people, programme: three reasons, one proof each.
explanation.trap: Repeating slogans from the bank's website: the interviewer knows them better than you do and recognises them immediately.
explanation.rule: A reason counts only if it cannot be transferred to a competitor.

questions.q: Why Investment Banking rather than Global Markets or Corporate Banking?
questions.tests: Whether you understand what each division really does and whether your choice comes from an informed comparison, not from the best-known name.
structure: Open with what the IB division concretely does: M&A and capital transactions, models, client materials, processes with many stakeholders
Show your proof: where you have already done that work and what you enjoyed
Compare the alternatives respectfully: what attracts you less in Markets (short horizon, continuous flow) or in Corporate Banking (recurring lending relationship)
Close with the 3-5 year trajectory that only this division gives you
good: A correct description of the day-to-day work of each division
The comparison is based on your preferences, not on a value judgement about the other divisions
A link to the M&A experience you already have
pitfalls: Belittling the other divisions ('trading is just gambling')
Confusing IB with asset management or direct investing
Having no answer if the question becomes 'and if we offered you Markets?'
questions.skeleton: Investment banking is where I can do what I have enjoyed most at [boutique]: understanding a business in depth, building [valuation models], and working on a transaction for [months] until it closes. Markets is fascinating, but its horizon is [minutes and days], while I am motivated by [long, project-based work with a defined outcome]. Corporate banking builds long relationships around [lending and transaction services], but I want to be closer to [strategic decisions like M&A]. In three to five years I want to [lead execution on cross-border tech deals], and IB is the direct path there.

steps: Check that you described the division with concrete activities, not adjectives.
Make sure the comparison with the other divisions is respectful and based on your work preferences.
Make sure the close points to a goal that only IB makes possible.
explanation.shortcut: What the job is, my proof, why not the alternatives, where I want to get to.
explanation.trap: Saying why you dislike the other divisions without explaining why you like IB: it looks like a choice by elimination.
explanation.rule: Choose a division for what it does, not for what the others do not do.

questions.q: Why do you want to work in London rather than in Milan?
questions.tests: Whether your choice of city is professional and sustainable over time: the interviewer is wary of candidates who only want the name of the financial centre or who will go home after a year.
structure: Open with the professional reason: the depth of the market and the type of deals that go through London (cross-border, EMEA, sector coverage)
Link it to your sector: the tech and semis teams covering Europe are often based there
Add a credible personal element: international experience, language, a network you have already built
Close with your long-term commitment and the value you bring from Italy (coverage of Italian clients)
good: Reasons tied to deals and team structure, not to the appeal of the city
Presenting your Italian as an asset for Italian clients within an EMEA team
Signs that you will put down roots: you have already lived, studied or worked abroad
pitfalls: 'London is the financial capital of Europe' as the only reason
Giving the impression that Milan is a fallback or that you only want a short experience
Being caught unprepared if the interviewer raises the cost of living or the visa question
questions.skeleton: Professionally, [London] is where most [EMEA technology and semiconductor] mandates are run, so the team covers [more cross-border deals and a broader client base] than I see in [Milan]. At [boutique] I have worked on [deal with foreign buyers], and I want to be at the centre of those processes rather than at the edge. I would also bring something to an EMEA team: [Italian language and network, knowledge of the Italian mid-market]. On a personal level, I have [lived abroad / studied in English], and I see [London] as a long-term base, not a short stop.

steps: Check that the first reason is about the type of work and deals, not the city itself.
Make sure you have signalled stability: experience abroad, a long-term plan.
Consider whether you have turned being Italian into an advantage for the team.
explanation.shortcut: Deals, sector, value you bring, long-term commitment.
explanation.trap: Talking about quality of life or generic 'international experience': it sounds like a tourist's choice.
explanation.rule: You choose a city for the work done there, and to stay.

questions.q: Why should we hire you?
questions.tests: Whether you can summarise your value in a specific and confident way, without arrogance, and whether you know what the role requires.
structure: Open with the summary: 'Three things'
Point 1: technical skills already proven in practice (models, valuations, client materials)
Point 2: experience on real deals and knowledge of a sector (semis and deep tech)
Point 3: ability to perform under pressure and specific motivation for this bank, with a proof
Close with what you bring to the team from day one
good: Three numbered points, each with a verifiable fact
An explicit link to what the programme is looking for (resilience, precision, teamwork)
A confident but not arrogant tone: you talk about proof, not superiority
pitfalls: Comparing yourself to the other candidates, whom you do not know
Listing adjectives ('hard-working, passionate, detail-oriented') without proof
Being too modest and not saying clearly what you bring
questions.skeleton: Three things. First, I can contribute from day one: at [boutique] I have [built operating models, run comps, drafted materials] on [number] live deals, so my learning curve on execution is shorter. Second, I bring sector depth in [semiconductors and deep tech], which is relevant to [Bank]'s [technology coverage]. Third, I have shown I can perform under pressure: [short proof, e.g. graduated with top marks while working / delivered X in Y days]. I am here because I want to [goal], and I would bring the same [ownership] to your team.

steps: Count the facts: every point must have a number, a deal or a result, otherwise it is just an adjective.
Check that every point matches a requirement of the role.
Reread the tone: no comparison with other candidates.
explanation.shortcut: Three points: skills, experience, resilience under pressure, each with a proof.
explanation.trap: Answering 'because I am hard-working and passionate': these are adjectives everyone uses and no one proves.
explanation.rule: You state your value with proof, not with adjectives.

questions.q: Where do you see yourself in five years?
questions.tests: Whether your ambition is realistic and consistent with the bank's career path, and whether there is a risk that you will leave soon.
structure: Open with your growth goal within the bank: from analyst to associate, with more responsibility on deals
Specify what you want to be able to do: lead execution, manage part of the client relationship, coordinate more junior analysts
Indicate a consistent specialisation: tech or semis coverage in EMEA
Close by linking the goal to what the programme offers
good: Concrete goals expressed in skills and responsibilities, not titles
Consistency with the bank's career structure
Clear but realistic ambition
pitfalls: Saying 'in a private equity fund' or 'running my own business'
Aiming for an unrealistic role, such as becoming an MD in 5 years
Answering 'I don't know, I am open to anything'
questions.skeleton: In five years I see myself as [an associate] in [the technology team] here, running day-to-day execution on [mid to large cap] deals, managing the analysts on the team and starting to own parts of the client relationship. By then I want to be the person the team relies on for [sector knowledge in semiconductors and deep tech]. The graduate programme is the right start because [training, rotations, exposure to senior bankers] would give me [specific skill] faster than anywhere else.

steps: Check that your goal is inside the bank and inside the division you are applying to.
Make sure you described skills and responsibilities, not just a title.
Make sure the programme is presented as the means to get there.
explanation.shortcut: Inside the bank, more responsibility, one sector, the programme as a springboard.
explanation.trap: Naming private equity as your goal: it signals that the programme is just a stepping stone.
explanation.rule: Your 5-year plan must make the bank's investment in you credible.

questions.q: You already work in M&A at a boutique. Why do you want to join a graduate programme?
questions.tests: Whether the choice is reasoned and not an escape, whether you accept restarting at entry level and whether you bring humility as well as experience.
structure: Open by recognising the value of your boutique experience: what you learned
Explain what you are looking for that the boutique cannot give you: deal size, products (ECM, DCM, leveraged finance), an international platform, structured training
Show humility: you are ready to start again from the basics and to learn the bank's way of working
Close with the advantage for them: a faster learning curve and the perspective of someone who has already done execution
good: Talking about what you are moving towards, never about what you are running from
Showing that you know what a large bank offers that a boutique does not
Explicit humility: no expectation of skipping levels
pitfalls: Criticising the boutique, your colleagues or your bosses
Giving the impression that you feel above graduate level
Having no answer if they ask 'why not apply as a lateral analyst?'
questions.skeleton: My time at [boutique] has been formative: I learned [valuation, process management, client materials] on [number] deals in [semiconductors and deep tech]. What a boutique cannot offer is [scale of transactions, access to financing products like DCM and leveraged finance, an international platform]. I want to see how [larger cross-border deals] are executed, with the structured training that [programme] offers. I am comfortable restarting at graduate level because [the breadth I would gain is worth it], and I think I can add value quickly because [I have already run parts of live processes].

steps: Check that there is no negative sentence about the boutique: even one shifts attention to a possible problem.
Make sure you have named at least two concrete things that only a large bank offers.
Make sure the message 'I am willing to start again' is explicit, not implicit.
explanation.shortcut: What I learned, what I am missing, why here, why I am ready to start again.
explanation.trap: Over-emphasising your experience to the point of seeming overqualified or unwilling to accept basic tasks.
explanation.rule: When you move on, talk about where you are going, not about what you are leaving.

questions.q: What do you know about our graduate programme?
questions.tests: Whether you have studied the structure of the programme and whether its features match what you are looking for.
structure: Open with the structure: length, divisions or rotations, locations
Training: the initial training period and what it includes
What sets it apart: mobility, client exposure, mentors or sponsors, type of deals
Close by explaining which feature matters most to you and why
good: Precise and correct details taken from the website, events or conversations
A personal link: which part of the programme you need most
A smart question for the end of the interview, prompted by this research
pitfalls: Reciting the website from memory with no personal comment
Confusing the programme with another bank's
Not knowing the length or the basic structure
questions.skeleton: The programme starts with [number] weeks of training in [location], covering [accounting, modelling, products], and then places analysts directly into [the team or a rotation]. What stood out to me is [specific feature, e.g. early client exposure, cross-border mobility, a mentoring scheme]. When I spoke to [a current analyst at an event], they told me [specific insight]. For me, the most valuable part is [feature], because [link to your development need, e.g. broader product knowledge after a boutique].

steps: Check that every fact you cite is correct and specific to that bank.
Make sure you have added at least one impression gathered from a person, not just from the website.
Make sure you close with why that feature matters to you.
explanation.shortcut: Structure, training, distinctive feature, why it matters to me.
explanation.trap: Stopping at the description: without the personal link, the research does not demonstrate motivation.
explanation.rule: Knowing the programme only helps if you explain why it suits you.

questions.q: Why do you want to cover the technology sector?
questions.tests: Whether your interest in the sector is deep and informed, and whether you can link it to M&A dynamics.
structure: Open with the underlying reason: a sector where strategy changes quickly and M&A is a central tool
Bring your proof: deals you worked on at the boutique in semis and deep tech
Show knowledge: 2 concrete M&A drivers in the sector (access to technology and talent, consolidation, supply-chain security)
Close with the value you bring to the team and a note of openness towards other sectors
good: Concrete sector drivers, not 'tech is the future'
Direct experience described with a technical detail
Openness to being allocated elsewhere if the programme provides for it
pitfalls: Talking only about consumer products or newspaper headlines
Seeming rigid: 'I only want tech'
Being unable to distinguish the sub-segments (design, foundry, equipment, software)
questions.skeleton: Technology is the sector where strategy and M&A are most connected: companies buy [capabilities, IP and talent] they cannot build fast enough. At [boutique] I have worked on [semiconductor / deep-tech deals], where the key questions were [technology roadmap, customer concentration, supply-chain exposure]. I find that combination of [technical diligence and valuation] genuinely interesting. Right now I am following [trend, e.g. consolidation in a sub-segment], which I think will drive [deal activity]. I would bring that sector knowledge, while staying open to [other coverage areas] in the programme.

steps: Check that you cited at least one sector-specific M&A driver.
Make sure the boutique experience is described with a concrete detail.
Make sure you closed with openness, not with rigid exclusivity.
explanation.shortcut: Why the sector, my proof, two drivers, openness.
explanation.trap: Confusing a technology user's enthusiasm with a banker's understanding of the sector.
explanation.rule: Interest in a sector means knowing why companies buy and sell in that sector.

questions.q: What is your greatest weakness?
questions.tests: Self-awareness and honesty: whether you recognise a real limitation, whether you are working on it methodically and whether the limitation is not fatal for the role.
structure: Open with a real and specific weakness that is not fatal for the role
Give a short example in which the weakness had an effect
Explain what you are doing to improve it, with a concrete method
Close with a measurable sign of improvement
good: A genuine limitation, for example asking for help too late, delegating too little, speaking up too little in meetings with senior colleagues
A concrete and verifiable corrective action
A calm tone, neither defensive nor overly self-critical
pitfalls: Fake weaknesses such as 'I am a perfectionist' or 'I work too hard'
A weakness incompatible with the role, such as poor attention to detail or difficulty with deadlines
Stopping at the weakness with no improvement plan
questions.skeleton: Earlier in my career I found it hard to [ask for help early / push back on a senior / delegate], because [reason]. On [deal or project], this meant [concrete consequence, e.g. I spent a night on something a colleague could have fixed in 20 minutes]. Since then I have [specific method, e.g. set myself a 30-minute rule before escalating, asked my VP for feedback every week]. The result is [measurable sign, e.g. fewer late surprises, positive feedback in my review], although I still [consciously check this when deadlines are tight].

steps: Check that the weakness is real: if it sounds like a disguised strength, the interviewer dismisses it.
Make sure it does not touch the key competencies of the role (precision, reliability, integrity).
Make sure there is an improvement method and proof that it works.
explanation.shortcut: Real weakness, example, method, proof of improvement.
explanation.trap: 'I am a perfectionist': it is the most overused answer and is read as a lack of self-awareness.
explanation.rule: A well-told weakness demonstrates your ability to improve.

questions.q: Why do you want to work in private credit rather than in investment banking?
questions.tests: Whether you understand the work of a private credit fund (originating, analysing and structuring loans, monitoring the portfolio) and whether your motivation comes from the role of the credit investor, not from a generic 'buy-side'.
structure: Open with what a private credit investor does: it lends directly to companies, often owned by private equity funds, and carries the risk until repayment
Explain what attracts you: an investor's perspective, focus on the downside, structure and covenants, a long-term relationship
Link your experience: business analysis, models and due diligence in M&A are the foundation of credit analysis
Close by acknowledging what you would miss about banking and why the trade-off convinces you
good: A credit mindset: 'how do we get repaid?' before 'how much can it grow?'
Knowledge of the key terms: leverage, interest cover, covenants, security, unitranche
Honestly acknowledging the trade-off compared with IB
pitfalls: Describing private credit as private equity under another name
Justifying the choice with better hours
Not knowing what a covenant is or how leverage is measured
questions.skeleton: In M&A I help clients [sell or buy companies]; in private credit I would be the one taking [the risk], which changes the question from 'what is this worth' to 'how and when do we get repaid'. I enjoy that discipline: at [boutique], the part I found most interesting was [diligence on cash generation, customer concentration, downside cases]. Private credit lets me apply it as an investor, structuring [leverage, covenants and security] and following the company for [several years]. I will miss [the variety of deals], but I prefer [owning an investment decision over its whole life].

steps: Check that you described the fund's work as a lender, not as a shareholder.
Make sure you used at least two credit concepts correctly (leverage, covenants, interest cover, security).
Make sure the trade-off compared with banking is stated honestly.
explanation.shortcut: Lender, not shareholder: downside, structure, repayment.
explanation.trap: Using the private equity answer ('I want to invest and create value'): in credit the return is capped and what matters is protecting capital.
explanation.rule: In credit, the first question is always how you get repaid.

questions.q: Walk me through the key decisions on your CV. Why did you make each one?
questions.tests: Whether your choices have a logic, whether you can explain them coherently and whether you learned something from each step.
structure: Open with the logic common to all your choices, in one sentence
Decision 1: degree and university, with the why
Decision 2: first experiences (internships, activities), with what they taught you
Decision 3: your current role at the boutique and why that sector
Close with the next decision: why this programme is consistent with the previous ones
good: Every choice has an explicit why and a lesson
Consistency: the choices build on one another
Naturally admitting a choice you would make differently, if there is one
pitfalls: Presenting your choices as random ('it just happened')
Justifying them after the fact in an unconvincing way
Dwelling on the early steps and reaching the present too late
questions.skeleton: Each step has been about [getting closer to transactions and technology]. I chose [your MSc] because [reason], and it gave me [skill]. During my studies I [internship or activity], where I learned [lesson] and realised I wanted [M&A]. I then joined [boutique] because it let me [work on live deals early and specialise in semiconductors]. Looking back, I would [one thing you would do differently]. Joining [Bank]'s programme is the logical next step because [scale, product breadth, international exposure].

steps: Check that every step has a why and a lesson, not just a date.
Make sure the story spends more time on the present than on the distant past.
Make sure the latest choice (this programme) is the natural consequence of the previous ones.
explanation.shortcut: One common thread, three decisions with the why, the next decision.
explanation.trap: Listing your experiences without explaining the choices: the question asks why, not what.
explanation.rule: A convincing CV is a sequence of reasoned choices, not of events.

questions.q: What other firms are you applying to?
questions.tests: The consistency of your search and your honesty: whether you are applying to similar roles for similar reasons, and how much demand there is for you on the market.
structure: Open honestly: you are considering similar roles at a few banks
State the common criterion: the same type of role (IB, tech coverage, EMEA)
Name at most 2-3 comparable firms, without rankings
Close by reaffirming why this bank is among your top choices, with a specific reason
good: Consistency: all applications are for the same type of role
Honesty about the status of your processes, without exaggerating
Reaffirming your specific interest in this bank
pitfalls: Listing inconsistent roles (consulting, trading, audit) that make your choice look random
Inventing non-existent offers to create pressure
Saying 'only you': rarely credible
questions.skeleton: I am focusing on [investment banking graduate roles at banks with a strong technology franchise in EMEA], so I am in process with [two or three comparable banks]. The common thread is [M&A execution on larger, cross-border deals], which is what I want after [my time at boutique]. I am at [stage] with them. [Bank] is among my first choices because [specific reason from your research], and I would be very happy to continue the process here.

steps: Check that your other applications are consistent with the role you are interviewing for.
Make sure you have not exaggerated the status of your processes.
Make sure you close with a specific reason for this bank.
explanation.shortcut: Same role, a few comparable banks, you among my top choices and why.
explanation.trap: Naming applications that are very different from one another: it suggests you do not know what you want.
explanation.rule: Consistent applications are proof of motivation.

questions.q: What do you want to achieve in your first twelve months here?
questions.tests: Whether you have realistic expectations for the first year and whether you know what makes an analyst reliable in the team's eyes.
structure: Open with the main goal: becoming an analyst the team can count on
Goal 1: mastering the bank's standards (models, formatting, internal processes)
Goal 2: exposure to products that are new compared with the boutique (financing, ECM, DCM)
Goal 3: building relationships within the team and with colleagues in other offices
Close with how you will measure success: feedback, responsibilities given to you, deals closed
good: Concrete and observable goals
Humility: learning the bank's methods before proposing changes
A focus on being useful to the team, not only on your own growth
pitfalls: Unrealistic goals, such as bringing in deals or managing clients in the first year
Vague goals such as 'learn as much as possible'
Talking only about what you want to receive and not about what you want to give
questions.skeleton: My main goal is to become an analyst the team can rely on without second-checking. In practice: first, master [Bank]'s standards for [models, pitch materials and internal processes] within [the first months]; second, get exposure to [products I did not see at a boutique, e.g. financing and capital markets]; third, build strong relationships with [the analyst class and senior bankers]. I would measure success by [the feedback in my first review and being trusted with larger parts of a deal].

steps: Check that the goals are compatible with a first-year analyst role.
Make sure every goal is measurable or at least observable.
Make sure at least one goal is about your contribution to the team.
explanation.shortcut: Reliability, new products, relationships, measure of success.
explanation.trap: Promising to bring in clients or generate deals: it reveals little understanding of the role.
explanation.rule: An analyst's first year is measured in reliability.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you worked in a team to achieve a difficult goal.
questions.tests: How you contribute to a team: your specific role, how you coordinate and communicate, and whether you put the common goal ahead of your own.
structure: Situation: the team, the goal and why it was difficult (1-2 sentences)
Task: your precise role in the team
Action: 2-3 things you did to make the team work (division of work, communication, support for a colleague)
Result: the outcome with a number and the feedback you received
Close with what you learned about working in a team
good: 'I' for your actions and 'we' only for the outcome
An action that shows attention to others, not only to your own task
A measurable result
pitfalls: Telling everything in the plural without making clear what you did
Choosing a story with no real difficulty
Taking all the credit
questions.skeleton: At [boutique], we had [timeframe] to deliver [deliverable, e.g. a management presentation] for [sell-side process] with a team of [number]. My role was [building the financial section]. I [proposed splitting the work by section with a shared tracker], [checked in twice a day with the associate to unblock issues], and [helped a colleague finish the market section when they fell behind]. We delivered [on time], the client [outcome], and the VP [feedback]. I learned that [clear ownership and early check-ins] matter more than working longer hours.

steps: Count how many times you say 'I' in the actions: if 'we' prevails, the interviewer cannot assess you.
Check that the difficulty is clear and real in the first two sentences.
Make sure the result has a number and that the lesson applies to the new role.
explanation.shortcut: STAR with at least one action that helps others.
explanation.trap: Describing the project instead of your contribution to the team.
explanation.rule: In teamwork, what matters is how you made the team better, not only your own piece.

questions.q: Tell me about a time a team member was not pulling their weight.
questions.tests: Whether you address the problem directly and respectfully, look for the cause before judging and protect the team's result.
structure: Situation: project, deadline, the problem you observed (without judging the person)
Action 1: you speak privately with the colleague to understand the cause
Action 2: you propose a concrete solution (redistribution, support, interim deadlines)
Action 3: if needed, you involve the manager transparently
Result on the work and on the relationship, then the lesson
good: Looking for the cause before judging
A direct, private conversation as the first step
Escalation only after trying to resolve it, and without an accusatory tone
pitfalls: Silently doing the other person's work without addressing the problem
Going straight to the boss to complain
Speaking badly of the colleague during the interview
questions.skeleton: During [university project / deal], a [teammate] was consistently [missing internal deadlines], which put [deliverable] at risk. Rather than assume, I [spoke to them privately] and learned [cause, e.g. they were also staffed on another urgent deal]. We agreed to [move the most time-sensitive section to me and set a midday check-in]. I also [let the associate know about the new split so priorities were clear]. We delivered [on time], and [the relationship stayed good]. I learned to [address issues early and directly, assuming good intent first].

steps: Check that your first step is a conversation with the colleague, not an escalation.
Make sure you describe the person neutrally, without labels.
Make sure the result covers both the deliverable and the relationship.
explanation.shortcut: Understand the cause, speak directly, concrete solution, transparent escalation if needed.
explanation.trap: Covering for the colleague by working through the night: it seems generous, but it does not solve the problem and hides the risk from the team.
explanation.rule: Address team problems early, in private and assuming good faith.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you worked with people from different backgrounds or locations.
questions.tests: Whether you can work in international and diverse teams: adapting your communication, respecting different styles and time zones, valuing different perspectives.
structure: Situation: the team (countries, cultures, functions) and the goal
Challenge: a concrete difference (communication style, time zone, language, expectations)
Action: how you adapted your way of working
Result with a measurable outcome
Close with what you learned about diversity as an advantage
good: A concrete difference described respectfully
Active adaptation of your own behaviour
Recognising the value that diversity added to the result
pitfalls: Cultural stereotypes
Saying 'there were no differences, we all got along'
Telling a story in which it was the others who had to adapt to you
questions.skeleton: On [cross-border deal], I worked with [the buyer's team in country, lawyers in country and our client in Italy]. The challenge was [different communication styles: the buyer expected short written updates, the client preferred calls]. I [set up a single tracker and a weekly written summary], [scheduled calls in the overlap between time zones], and [confirmed key points in writing after each call]. As a result, [diligence questions were closed in X days instead of Y]. I learned that [adapting my style] is part of the job, and that [the buyer's perspective] improved our materials.

steps: Check that you described a concrete difference without generalising about cultures.
Make sure you are the one adapting, with specific actions.
Make sure the result shows a concrete benefit.
explanation.shortcut: Concrete difference, my adaptation, benefit to the result.
explanation.trap: Reducing diversity to an obstacle to overcome rather than a resource.
explanation.rule: In international teams, whoever adapts first leads the collaboration.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you took the lead.
questions.tests: Whether you take responsibility when needed, and can give direction, involve others and deliver a result.
structure: Situation: why someone needed to lead
Task: why you were the one to do it
Action: how you gave direction (clear goal, division of tasks, decisions)
Action: how you involved and motivated the others
Result with a number and what you learned about leadership
good: Leadership as service to the group, not as command
Clear and reasoned decisions
A moment when you listened or changed your mind
pitfalls: Confusing leadership with doing everything yourself
Stories in which the formal title is the only proof
No reference to how the others reacted
questions.skeleton: In [context, e.g. a university case competition / student association], our team of [number] had [timeframe] to [goal], and after the first week we had [no clear plan]. I [offered to coordinate]: I [split the task into workstreams based on each person's strengths], [set two short check-ins a week], and [made the final call on our recommendation when we were split, after hearing both sides]. We [result, e.g. reached the final / delivered on time], and [feedback]. I learned that leading means [creating clarity for others], not doing everything myself.

steps: Check that there is a moment when you made a difficult decision for the group.
Make sure you showed how you involved the others, not just what you decided.
Make sure the result belongs to the group and is measurable.
explanation.shortcut: Clarity was needed, I created it, I involved the others, we achieved the result.
explanation.trap: Telling a story in which you are the lone hero: for assessors it is a sign of weak leadership.
explanation.rule: A leader creates clarity and responsibility for others.

questions.q: Describe a time you had to lead or influence people without formal authority.
questions.tests: Whether you can get results by coordinating more senior or external people (clients, lawyers, auditors) who do not report to you, an everyday situation for an analyst.
structure: Situation: whom you had to coordinate and why you had no authority
Goal: what you needed to achieve and by when
Action: making it easy to collaborate (clear requests, deadlines, drafts ready)
Action: building credibility through preparation and follow-up, escalating through your senior
Result and lesson on how to influence without hierarchy
good: Concrete tools: trackers, specific requests, preparation that saves others time
Respect for other people's roles and timelines
Escalation used with judgement, through your own senior
pitfalls: Saying you 'put pressure' on senior people
Going around the hierarchy without involving your own manager
Having no clear result
questions.skeleton: During [sell-side process], I ran [the data room and buyer Q&A], which meant getting answers from [the client's CFO, the lawyers and the auditors], none of whom reported to me. Answers took [X days] and buyers were [frustrated]. I [grouped questions by owner and priority], [sent each person a short list with a clear deadline and a draft answer where possible], and [flagged the three blocking items to my VP for the weekly client call]. Response time fell to [Y days] and [the process stayed on schedule]. I learned that [making it easy to help you] is the best way to influence.

steps: Check that the people involved were genuinely outside your authority.
Make sure your actions make it easier to collaborate rather than increasing the pressure.
Make sure the result is measurable (timings, deadlines met).
explanation.shortcut: Make it easy to collaborate, build credibility, escalate through your senior.
explanation.trap: Describing influence as insistence: with senior people and clients, insistence without added value is counterproductive.
explanation.rule: Without authority, you lead through preparation and clarity.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you helped develop someone more junior.
questions.tests: Whether you can transfer knowledge, give feedback and help others grow, something an analyst already does with interns and new joiners.
structure: Situation: who the person was and what they needed to learn
Action: how you explained (practical example, checklist, joint review)
Action: how you gave feedback and gradually increased their autonomy
Result: what they could do afterwards and the impact on the team
Close with what you learned yourself
good: A concrete method (guided example, checklist, short sessions)
Specific and constructive feedback
A balance between helping and leaving autonomy
pitfalls: Redoing the other person's work instead of teaching
A patronising tone towards the person
No proof that the person improved
questions.skeleton: When [an intern] joined [boutique] during [a busy period], they were asked to [update the trading comps] but had never [used our data provider or template]. I [walked them through one company end to end], [gave them a short checklist of the five most common errors], and [reviewed their first output with them line by line instead of fixing it myself]. Within [two weeks] they were [producing comps that needed only minor comments], which freed [X hours] of my time each week. I learned that [ten minutes of explaining] saves hours of correcting.

steps: Check that you showed a teaching method, not just willingness.
Make sure there is proof of the person's progress.
Make sure the benefit to the team comes through.
explanation.shortcut: Show, give a tool, review together, measure progress.
explanation.trap: Saying you corrected the work yourself: it is efficient today but helps no one grow.
explanation.rule: Developing someone means making them able to do it without you.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you disagreed with your manager.
questions.tests: Whether you can express disagreement respectfully and with data, at the right time and in the right way, and then accept and execute the final decision.
structure: Situation: what you disagreed on and why it mattered
Action: you prepared evidence before raising it
Action: you chose the right moment and a respectful tone, proposing an alternative
Result: the decision taken (even if not in your favour) and how you followed through
Close with the lesson
good: Disagreement based on data, not opinions
Respect for the hierarchy: you propose, you do not impose
Willingness to accept the final decision and execute it well
pitfalls: Saying you were right and the boss was wrong, with a tone of vindication
Disagreement expressed in front of the client
Being unable to find an example: it comes across as passivity
questions.skeleton: On [deal], my VP wanted to [use a specific peer set] for the valuation. I thought [two of the peers had a very different business model], which would [overstate the multiple by about X turns]. Before raising it, I [prepared a one-page comparison of both peer sets]. I [asked for five minutes after the internal call], explained the impact and suggested [showing both sets]. The VP [decision]. Either way, I [executed the agreed approach quickly]. I learned that [disagreement backed by data, raised in private and with an alternative] is welcomed.

steps: Check that the disagreement is supported by concrete analysis.
Check the setting and the tone: in private, respectfully, proposing an alternative.
Make sure you show that you would have executed the decision even if it differed from your proposal.
explanation.shortcut: Data, a private moment, an alternative, respect for the decision.
explanation.trap: Choosing a story in which the manager was obviously wrong: it sounds like criticism and does not show maturity.
explanation.rule: Good disagreement comes with data, in private, with a proposal.

questions.q: Describe a conflict with a colleague and how you resolved it.
questions.tests: Managing relationships under pressure: the ability to listen, separate the person from the problem and find a solution that lasts.
structure: Situation: the conflict described neutrally, without blame
Action: you tried to understand the other person's perspective
Action: you proposed a concrete agreement on how to work
Result: the outcome for the work and for the relationship
Lesson about conflict
good: A neutral description and shared responsibility
Active listening and questions to understand the other point of view
A practical and lasting solution
pitfalls: Describing the colleague as the 'villain'
Personal conflicts unrelated to work
A resolution left entirely to a third party
questions.skeleton: On [project], another analyst and I [were both editing the same model], and we kept [overwriting each other's changes], which led to [tension and a version error]. I [suggested a short call] and asked how they saw it; they felt [I was changing their sections without telling them]. That was fair. We agreed [clear ownership of each tab, a change log and one master file]. After that, [there were no further version errors], and we [worked well together on the next two deals]. I learned to [address friction early and focus on the process, not the person].

steps: Check that the story also admits your share of responsibility.
Make sure there is a concrete solution about the way of working.
Make sure the relationship came out stronger, or at least working.
explanation.shortcut: Neutrality, listening, practical agreement, relationship preserved.
explanation.trap: Showing that you were completely right: it signals poor self-awareness.
explanation.rule: In a conflict you solve the problem; you do not win against the person.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you dealt with a difficult client or counterparty.
questions.tests: Professionalism with external counterparts: calm, an understanding of the client's real interests, and the ability to protect the relationship and the process without overstepping your remit.
structure: Situation: who the client or counterparty was and what made the situation difficult
Action: you understood the real interest behind the request
Action: you responded with facts, options and clear timelines, involving your senior when needed
Result for the process and the relationship
Lesson on client management
good: Calm and respect even when the client is hostile
Distinguishing between the stated position and the real interest
Involving your senior for decisions outside your remit
pitfalls: Making commitments to the client without consulting the team
Speaking badly of the client
Saying you gave in on everything just to avoid conflict
questions.skeleton: On [sell-side mandate], the [client's founder] was [unhappy with the valuation range in our first draft] and [called me directly late one evening]. I listened without arguing and realised the real concern was [that a competitor had sold at a higher multiple]. I [prepared a short comparison of growth and margins between the two businesses], [reviewed it with my VP], and we [walked the client through it the next morning, together with an upside case]. The client [accepted the range and became more engaged in the process]. I learned to [separate the emotion from the underlying question].

steps: Check that you identified the real interest behind the complaint.
Make sure you did not make commitments on your own: significant decisions go through your senior.
Make sure the result includes the relationship with the client.
explanation.shortcut: Listen, find the real interest, respond with facts, involve your senior.
explanation.trap: Saying you satisfied the client by changing the numbers: it looks like a lack of integrity.
explanation.rule: With a difficult client, facts and calm are worth more than concessions.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you made a mistake.
questions.tests: Integrity and ownership: whether you admit the mistake immediately, limit the damage, understand its cause and change your process.
structure: Situation: the mistake, stated directly and without minimising it
Immediate action: you reported it straight away to your manager
Action: you corrected it and limited the impact
Action: you understood the cause and introduced a check to prevent it
Result and proof that the check worked afterwards
good: A real but not catastrophic mistake
Immediate and transparent reporting
A concrete and permanent change to your work process
pitfalls: Choosing a fake mistake or one made by others
Minimising it or blaming external circumstances
Not explaining what you do differently today
questions.skeleton: On [deal], I sent my associate [a draft comps page] in which [the EBITDA of two peers came from the wrong fiscal year], which [moved the median EV/EBITDA by about X turns]. I spotted it [an hour later] and told him straight away, with the corrected page, before it reached [the client]. The root cause was [that my process had no check on periods]. Since then I [run a five-point checklist before sending anything, including periods, units and currencies], and it has [caught several issues since]. I learned that [flagging early] protects both the team and trust.

steps: Check that the mistake is yours and that you tell it without excuses.
Make sure the reporting was immediate and transparent.
Make sure you describe the permanent change to your process.
explanation.shortcut: Mistake, reported immediately, corrected, cause found, process changed.
explanation.trap: Choosing a 'mistake' that is really a strength, such as 'I worked too hard': the interviewer reads it as evasion.
explanation.rule: In banking, a mistake flagged immediately is manageable; a hidden one is not.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you failed.
questions.tests: Resilience and the ability to learn: how you react to a significant negative outcome and what you change afterwards.
structure: Situation: an important goal you did not achieve
Your part: what depended on you, stated honestly
Reaction: how you handled the moment and asked for feedback
Concrete lesson
Subsequent result: where you applied the lesson successfully
good: A genuine failure, with real consequences
Personal responsibility without self-flagellation
Proof that you applied the lesson in a later situation
pitfalls: A fake or tiny 'failure'
Blaming others or bad luck entirely
No lesson, or a generic one such as 'never give up'
questions.skeleton: [On a pitch at boutique / In a competition at university], we [aimed for specific goal] and [did not achieve it: our pitch lost to a competitor]. Looking back, my part was [that I focused on the model and spent too little time understanding what the client actually wanted]. It was [disappointing], but I [asked the client contact and my MD for feedback]. The lesson was [start from the client's question, then build the analysis]. On the next pitch, I [drafted the key messages first and built the analysis around them], and we [won the mandate / received strong feedback].

steps: Check that the failure is real and that your share of responsibility is clear.
Make sure the lesson is specific and not a generic motto.
Make sure you close with a later situation in which the lesson worked.
explanation.shortcut: Real failure, my part, specific lesson, later success.
explanation.trap: Stopping at the failure: without the positive follow-up, the story shows only the problem.
explanation.rule: A failure shows your ability to learn, not your limitations.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you received critical feedback.
questions.tests: Whether you accept feedback without getting defensive, turn it into action and show visible progress.
structure: Situation: who gave you the feedback and on what
Reaction: you listened and asked questions to understand
Action: the concrete plan to improve
Result: how the next assessment changed
Close with your relationship with feedback today
good: Real feedback that is relevant to the role
A mature reaction, without excuses
Proof of the change
pitfalls: Trivial feedback, or feedback that is actually a compliment
Saying you disputed the feedback
Not showing the improvement
questions.skeleton: After [my first months at boutique], my VP told me that [my pages were analytically correct but the key message was buried]. My first instinct was [to explain why], but instead I [asked for two examples and for what good looked like]. I then [started writing the headline of each page before building it, and asked for a quick review of my first draft on the next deal]. In my next review, [the same VP said my materials needed far fewer comments]. Since then I [ask for feedback at the end of every deal].

steps: Check that the feedback is substantive and work-related.
Make sure your reaction was to listen and act, not to defend yourself.
Make sure you close with proof of the improvement.
explanation.shortcut: Feedback, listening, plan, proof of improvement.
explanation.trap: Saying the feedback was unfair: even if it was, in an interview it signals a closed mindset.
explanation.rule: Feedback is worth what you do with it afterwards.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you worked under significant pressure.
questions.tests: How you keep quality and composure when time pressure and stakes are high: organisation, prioritisation, communication.
structure: Situation: the deadline and the stakes, in concrete terms
Action: you organised the work and set priorities
Action: you protected quality with targeted checks
Action: you flagged risks and progress early
Result with a number, and the lesson
good: An explicit method (priorities, hour-by-hour plan, checks)
Composure and proactive communication
Quality maintained despite the pressure
pitfalls: Only saying that you worked through the night
Conveying panic or chaos
Not saying how you checked quality
questions.skeleton: On [deal], the [bid deadline was moved forward by X days], so we had [48 hours] to [update the model and the valuation materials]. I [listed every deliverable, ranked them by what the client would read first, and agreed the order with my associate]. I [built the model updates first, then the pages], and [kept the last 30 minutes for a full check of numbers across the document]. I [sent short progress updates every few hours]. We [delivered on time with no errors], and [outcome]. I learned that [a clear plan in the first hour] is what keeps pressure under control.

steps: Check that the method is visible: priorities, sequence, checks.
Check that you showed proactive communication with the team.
Make sure the result includes quality, not just meeting the deadline.
explanation.shortcut: Plan, priorities, quality check, updates.
explanation.trap: Using hours worked as evidence: working long hours does not prove you can handle pressure.
explanation.rule: Under pressure, whoever plans in the first hour wins.

questions.q: Describe a time you had to manage competing priorities from different people.
questions.tests: Whether you can handle conflicting requests from several seniors without promising everything: transparency, prioritisation criteria, renegotiating deadlines.
structure: Situation: who was asking for what, and why the requests were incompatible
Action: you estimated the time, urgency and impact of each
Action: you made the conflict transparent to the seniors and proposed an order
Action: you delivered and kept everyone updated
Result and lesson
good: Transparency: the seniors are informed of the conflict
Proposing a solution, not just flagging the problem
Meeting the renegotiated deadlines
pitfalls: Saying yes to everyone and delivering late
Setting priorities on your own without telling anyone
Complaining about the workload
questions.skeleton: On the same afternoon, [my VP on deal A asked for a revised model by 9am] and [an MD on a pitch asked for a market page by the same time]. I could not deliver both properly. I [estimated each task at about X hours], then [wrote to both with a proposed plan: the model first because the client call was at 10am, the market page by noon, or support from another analyst]. The MD [agreed to noon]. I [delivered both as agreed]. I learned that [making the trade-off visible early] beats silently trying to do everything.

steps: Check that you made the conflict visible to the seniors involved.
Check that your proposal follows a clear criterion (client deadline, impact).
Make sure the renegotiated deadlines were met.
explanation.shortcut: Estimate, criterion, transparent proposal, delivery.
explanation.trap: Silently accepting everything: it looks like willingness but leads to missed deadlines or lower quality.
explanation.rule: Competing priorities are resolved by making them visible, not by hiding them.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you missed, or nearly missed, a deadline.
questions.tests: Honesty and risk management: whether you recognise the problem early, give timely warning with a plan and change your method for the future.
structure: Situation: the deadline and why it was at risk
Recognition: when you realised you would not make it and what you did immediately
Action: timely warning with an alternative plan (partial delivery, help, new deadline)
Result: limited impact
Lesson and change in how you estimate or plan
good: Honesty about the delay
Early warning, not at the last minute
A structural change in your planning method
pitfalls: Denying that you have ever put a deadline at risk
Blaming others
Only giving warning after the deadline
questions.skeleton: On [project], I [underestimated how long it would take to collect data for X companies] and, [two days before the deadline], I realised I would not finish properly. I [told my associate immediately], [proposed delivering the core analysis on time and the remaining companies a day later], and [asked whether another analyst could take part of the data work]. The client [received the core output on time, with no impact on the process]. Since then I [break tasks into steps with time estimates and check progress at the halfway point], so [I flag risks much earlier].

steps: Check that you admitted the delay directly.
Check when you gave warning: the earlier, the better.
Make sure you describe the change of method that prevents it.
explanation.shortcut: Recognise early, warn with a plan, limit the impact, change your method.
explanation.trap: Answering 'I have never missed a deadline': it is not credible and skips the competency they want to assess.
explanation.rule: A deadline at risk flagged early is a planning problem, not a trust problem.

questions.q: Give an example of when your attention to detail made a difference.
questions.tests: Whether quality control is part of how you work and whether you can explain the impact of an error avoided.
structure: Situation: the deliverable and why accuracy mattered
Action: your checking method (tying out the numbers, comparison with sources, consistency across pages)
What you found: the error or inconsistency, in concrete terms
Result: the impact avoided, with a number
Close with how the method became a habit
good: A systematic checking method, not luck
An error with a quantifiable impact
An established habit, shared with the team
pitfalls: Vague stories ('I always double-check')
Trivial errors such as a typo
Coming across as slow or overly perfectionist
questions.skeleton: Before [a board presentation on deal], I was [checking that the numbers in the executive summary matched the model]. I always [tie every number on a page back to its source]. I noticed that [the net debt on the summary page was from the previous quarter], which [misstated the implied equity value by about X million]. I [corrected it, checked every other page that used net debt, and told my associate what I had changed]. The client saw [consistent numbers], and [the VP added my tie-out step to the team's checklist].

steps: Check that the story shows a repeatable method, not a stroke of luck.
Check that the error has a quantified impact.
Make sure you said how you communicated the correction.
explanation.shortcut: Method, error found, impact avoided, habit.
explanation.trap: Talking about finding a typo: it does not demonstrate the accuracy needed on numbers and models.
explanation.rule: Accuracy is proven with a method, not an intention.

questions.q: How do you check your work before sending it to a senior?
questions.tests: Whether you have a concrete, repeatable checking process: it is a practical question and the answer must be a method, not a promise.
structure: Open by saying that you follow a fixed checklist
Check 1: numbers (tie-out to the model, sources, units, currencies, periods)
Check 2: logic (do the numbers make sense? comparison with the prior year and with peers, orders of magnitude)
Check 3: format (formatting, consistency across pages, footnotes and sources)
Close with the final step, rereading as the recipient would, and an example of an error caught this way
good: A concrete checklist of 3-5 points
A sanity check on orders of magnitude
A real example of an error caught
pitfalls: 'I read it twice' as the only check
No distinction between numbers, logic and format
Saying that checking is the senior's job
questions.skeleton: I use the same checklist every time. First, numbers: every figure [ties back to the model or the source], with [units, currency and period] checked. Second, logic: I ask whether the numbers make sense, for example [whether margins are in line with last year and with peers, and whether orders of magnitude are right]. Third, format: [consistent fonts, footnotes and sources across pages]. Finally, I [zoom out and read it as the client would]. Last month this [caught a revenue figure in thousands instead of millions] before it went to [my VP].

steps: Check that the method has at least three distinct levels: numbers, logic, format.
Check that you included a sanity check on orders of magnitude.
Make sure you gave a concrete example.
explanation.shortcut: Numbers, logic, format, read as the recipient.
explanation.trap: Describing the check as a generic reread: the senior wants to know what you check, not how many times.
explanation.rule: The first reviewer of your work is you, with a checklist.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you spotted an error made by someone more senior.
questions.tests: Courage and tact: whether you flag a senior's error quickly, discreetly and after verifying it, putting the quality of the work ahead of hierarchy.
structure: Situation: what you noticed and in which document
Verification: you double-checked before raising it
Action: you flagged it privately, quickly, with the evidence and a proposed fix
Result: error corrected before it went out
Lesson on how to flag issues upwards
good: Verification before flagging
Private, quick, non-accusatory communication
A correction already prepared
pitfalls: Flagging it in front of others or the client
Saying nothing for fear of the hierarchy
A superior tone in the story
questions.skeleton: While [preparing the final version of a valuation pack], I noticed that [the DCF the associate had built used the wrong tax rate], which [moved the valuation by about X%]. I [rechecked the source twice to be sure], then [messaged him privately with the figure, the source and a corrected version]. He [thanked me and updated it before it went to the client]. I learned that [seniors want to know quickly, privately and with a solution], and that [protecting the quality of what the client sees] matters more than hierarchy.

steps: Check that you verified the error before flagging it.
Check the channel: private and immediate.
Make sure you brought a solution, not just the problem.
explanation.shortcut: Verify, flag privately, bring the fix.
explanation.trap: Staying silent out of respect for the hierarchy: in a bank, an error that reaches the client harms everyone.
explanation.rule: Flag errors upwards quickly, privately and with the solution.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you persuaded someone to change their mind.
questions.tests: Whether you can influence with arguments built on the other person's priorities, listening to their objections, without imposing.
structure: Situation: whom you had to persuade and about what
Action: you understood what really mattered to the other person
Action: you built the argument on their criteria, with data
Action: you handled the main objection with a concrete proposal
Result and lesson
good: An argument built on the other person's priorities
Data and a concrete alternative
Respect for the other person's decision, whatever it was
pitfalls: Persuasion through insistence or hierarchy
Trivial stories with nothing at stake
Not mentioning the other person's objections
questions.skeleton: On [deal], the [client's CFO] wanted to [approach only strategic buyers], while we believed [adding two financial sponsors would create more competition]. With my VP, I [asked what worried him] and learned it was [confidentiality]. I [prepared a page showing recent sponsor deals in the sector at comparable multiples, and a proposal to share only a teaser with sponsors until they signed an NDA]. He [agreed to add three sponsors], and [one of them made the second-highest bid]. I learned that [persuasion starts from the other person's concern, not from my argument].

steps: Check that you identified the other person's real concern.
Check that the argument uses data and addresses that concern.
Make sure the result is concrete and verifiable.
explanation.shortcut: Understand their concern, respond with data, offer a way out.
explanation.trap: Saying you convinced someone by repeating your own view: that is not persuasion, it is pressure.
explanation.rule: You persuade by addressing the other person's concern.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you had to explain something complex to a non-expert.
questions.tests: Clarity: whether you can simplify without losing accuracy, adapting the message to the audience and checking that it landed.
structure: Situation: who the audience was and what you had to explain
Action: you started from the conclusion and from what mattered to them
Action: you used an analogy or an example with simple numbers
Action: you checked understanding with questions
Result and lesson
good: The key message in one sentence
A simple but correct analogy or numerical example
Actively checking understanding
pitfalls: Using technical jargon with a non-expert audience
Simplifying to the point of saying inaccurate things
Not checking whether the message landed
questions.skeleton: The [founder of a deep-tech client] was [an engineer] and could not see why buyers would value his company on [a multiple of revenue rather than on what it had spent on R&D]. I [started with the conclusion: buyers pay for future cash flows]. Then I [used a simple example: two companies with the same revenue, one growing at 40% a year and one at 10%, and showed how growth changed the price]. I [asked him to explain it back in his own words]. He [later used the same logic with his board]. I learned to [lead with the answer and use one example].

steps: Check that the key message comes across in the first two sentences.
Check that the example is simple but technically correct.
Make sure you checked that the other person had understood.
explanation.shortcut: Conclusion, simple example, check understanding.
explanation.trap: Explaining the whole technical process in order: the non-expert gets lost before reaching the point.
explanation.rule: Explain starting from the answer, then an example, then the details if needed.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you negotiated something.
questions.tests: Whether you prepare for a negotiation, know your room for manoeuvre and the other party's interests, and seek a deal that works for both sides.
structure: Situation: what was at stake and with whom
Preparation: your goal, your limit and the other party's interest
Action: opening proposal and exchange of concessions
Result: agreement reached, with a number
Lesson on negotiation
good: Explicit preparation (goal, limit, alternatives)
Concessions traded, not given away
An agreement that preserves the relationship
pitfalls: Describing a negotiation where you 'won' by humiliating the other side
Negotiations with nothing real at stake
No numbers
questions.skeleton: As [treasurer of a student association], I had to [agree terms with a corporate sponsor] for [our annual finance conference]. Before the meeting I [set a target of X, a walk-away point of Y, and listed what we could offer at little cost, such as visibility]. They opened at [figure]. Instead of simply pushing on price, I [traded a logo on our materials and a speaking slot for a higher contribution]. We closed at [figure, X% above their opening offer], and they [renewed the following year]. I learned that [preparation and trading concessions] matter more than tough talk.

steps: Check that you described the goal, the limit and the other party's interests before the negotiation.
Check that every concession was traded for something in return.
Make sure the result has a number and that the relationship stayed good.
explanation.shortcut: Goal, limit, traded concessions, measurable agreement.
explanation.trap: Confusing negotiation with toughness: interviewers are looking for preparation and creativity.
explanation.rule: Do not give concessions away: trade them.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you went beyond what was asked of you.
questions.tests: Ownership and proactivity: whether you do more when it adds real value, without neglecting the assigned task.
structure: Situation: what you had been asked to do
What you noticed was missing or could be improved
Action: what extra you did, after completing the main task
Result: concrete value for the team or the client
Lesson
good: The main task completed before the extra
The extra meets a real need, not a wish to get noticed
A measurable result
pitfalls: Extras that delayed the requested work
Initiatives taken without informing your manager when needed
Stories where the extra is just 'I worked more'
questions.skeleton: I was asked to [prepare a list of potential buyers for a semiconductor client]. After delivering it, I noticed [we had no view on which buyers had recently done similar deals or had the balance sheet to pay]. I [added a page ranking each buyer by recent M&A activity, net leverage and strategic fit] and [shared it with my associate as an optional addition]. The MD [used it in the client meeting to prioritise the first outreach], and [two of the top five buyers entered the process]. I learned that [the best initiative answers the next question the client will ask].

steps: Check that the requested task was completed before the initiative.
Check that the extra meets a concrete need.
Make sure the impact is visible and measured.
explanation.shortcut: Task done, need spotted, useful extra, impact.
explanation.trap: Describing an extra that nobody used: it shows commitment but not judgement.
explanation.rule: Initiative counts when it anticipates the client's next question.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you improved a process.
questions.tests: Whether you can spot an inefficiency, propose a concrete solution, win the buy-in of those who use it and measure its effect.
structure: Situation: the inefficient process and its cost (time, errors)
Action: the root-cause analysis
Action: the solution and how you involved those who had to use it
Result: time saved or errors avoided, with a number
Close with adoption by others
good: The cost of the problem quantified
Involving colleagues and your manager
A measured, lasting impact
pitfalls: Imposing the change without buy-in
Explaining the technical solution in excessive detail
No measure of the effect
questions.skeleton: At [boutique], updating [trading comps for each pitch] took [about X hours] because [data was copied by hand from different sources]. I [mapped the steps], then [built a template linked to our data provider, with standard definitions of EBITDA and net debt]. I [tested it on two pitches with my associate] before [proposing it to the team]. It [cut the update time to about Y hours] and [reduced definition errors]. It is now [the team's standard template]. I learned that [testing a change on a real case] is what gets people to adopt it.

steps: Check that you quantified the initial cost and the final saving.
Check that you involved the people using the process before changing it.
Make sure the improvement was adopted, not just proposed.
explanation.shortcut: Cost, cause, tested solution, adoption, number.
explanation.trap: Describing the technical solution in detail and forgetting impact and buy-in.
explanation.rule: A process truly improves when others adopt it.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you identified an opportunity that others had missed.
questions.tests: Curiosity and commercial awareness: whether you connect information in an original way and turn an insight into concrete action.
structure: Situation: the context and the starting information
The insight: what you connected that others had not seen
Action: how you tested the idea and whom you presented it to
Result: what came of it
Lesson
good: A clear logical link between data and opportunity
Testing the idea before presenting it
A concise pitch, going through your own manager
pitfalls: Vague or untested ideas
Presenting the idea by going over your manager's head
No concrete follow-up
questions.skeleton: While [reading the quarterly report of a mid-cap semiconductor company], I noticed [it had started reporting a non-core product line as a separate segment]. Combined with [management comments about refocusing the portfolio], it suggested [a possible carve-out]. I [built a quick view of the segment's revenue, margins and likely buyers] and [shared a one-page note with my VP]. We [used it to open a conversation with the company], and [it led to a follow-up meeting]. I learned that [reading primary sources closely] is where good ideas come from.

steps: Check that the link between information and opportunity is logical and explainable.
Check that you tested the idea with some analysis before proposing it.
Make sure there is a concrete follow-up.
explanation.shortcut: Data, connection, test, proposal, follow-up.
explanation.trap: Describing a brilliant idea that stayed an idea: the interviewer is also looking for execution.
explanation.rule: An opportunity counts when you turn it into a verifiable action.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you faced an ethical dilemma.
questions.tests: Integrity: whether you recognise an ethical problem, resist pressure and use the proper channels, even when the right choice has a cost.
structure: Situation: the dilemma, described in concrete terms
Why it was difficult: the pressure or the cost of the right choice
Action: what you did and which channels you used (manager, lecturer, compliance)
Result
The principle that guides your choices
good: A real dilemma with a cost attached to the right choice
Using the proper channels instead of deciding alone
A clear principle, consistent with the culture of a regulated bank
pitfalls: Trivial situations with no real dilemma
Stories in which you took part in the wrongdoing
Resolving everything alone without informing those who needed to know
questions.skeleton: During [a university group project], [a team member suggested reusing analysis from a previous year's submission that another group had shared]. It would have [saved us days], and [the team was under pressure]. I said I was not comfortable, explained [the risk for all of us], and suggested [we ask the professor what was allowed and rebuild the analysis from public sources]. We [did so], [lost two days but delivered on time], and [the issue was handled correctly]. My principle is simple: [if I would not be comfortable explaining it to a regulator or a client, I do not do it].

steps: Check that the dilemma has a real cost for the right choice.
Check that you used the proper channels (manager, lecturer, compliance).
Make sure you close with a clear principle.
explanation.shortcut: Dilemma, cost, proper channel, principle.
explanation.trap: Choosing a dilemma where the right answer was obvious and cost nothing: it proves nothing.
explanation.rule: In a regulated environment, the right choice goes through the right channels.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you challenged something you believed was wrong.
questions.tests: Courage and judgement: whether you can raise a problem constructively, even against the prevailing view or with a senior, with the facts on your side.
structure: Situation: what you believed was wrong and why
Verification: you checked the facts before acting
Action: you raised the issue with the right person, constructively
Result
Lesson on when and how to step in
good: Facts verified before acting
A constructive, solution-oriented tone
Choosing the right person and the right moment
pitfalls: Confusing personal preferences with matters of principle
Describing an open or public clash
Not showing the result
questions.skeleton: On [project], [a valuation page presented management's projections as our own base case], although [they assumed growth of X% a year, well above the market's Y%]. I felt it could [mislead the reader]. I [checked the market data again], then [raised it privately with my associate], suggesting [labelling the case as management's and adding a sensitivity at market growth].
