He [agreed and took it to the VP]. The final document [showed both cases clearly]. I learned that [challenging is easier when you bring evidence and a practical fix].

steps: Check that the issue is one of substance (correctness, transparency) and not of personal taste.
Check that you verified the facts before raising the issue.
Make sure you proposed a practical solution.
explanation.shortcut: Facts, right person, constructive tone, solution.
explanation.trap: Telling the story as a battle won against a superior: the emphasis should be on the correct outcome, not on winning.
explanation.rule: Challenge with evidence and a proposal, not with confrontation.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you had to keep information confidential under pressure.
questions.tests: Whether you understand the value of confidentiality in M&A (inside information, code names, need-to-know) and stay discreet even with friends and with colleagues from other teams.
structure: Situation: what type of information it was and who was pressing to find out
Why it was confidential and what was at risk
Action: how you handled the request without lying and without revealing anything
Action: you followed internal procedures (reporting to compliance, where required)
Close with the habits you use to protect information
good: Knowledge of the rules (inside information, need-to-know, code names)
A polite but firm answer, neither confirming nor denying
Concrete protective habits
pitfalls: Revealing identifiable details of the deal during the interview itself
Saying that you lied to protect the information
Underestimating the legal risk
questions.skeleton: On [a live M&A mandate for a listed company], [a friend working in asset management] asked me directly whether [the rumours about the company being for sale] were true. I [said I never discuss client work, without confirming or denying anything], and [moved the conversation on]. I also [reported the approach to compliance, as our procedures require]. More generally, I [use code names, never discuss work in public places, and keep files only on approved systems]. For me, confidentiality is [both a legal obligation and the basis of client trust].

steps: Check that you did not reveal anything identifiable about the deal, not even in your interview answer.
Check that your response to the request was firm but polite, neither confirming nor denying.
Make sure you mentioned concrete habits and reporting to compliance where required.
explanation.shortcut: Neither confirm nor deny, report where required, protective habits.
explanation.trap: Telling the story with the client's name or identifiable details: it contradicts the very competency being assessed.
explanation.rule: In M&A, confidentiality is a legal obligation before it is a virtue.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you had to adapt to a significant change.
questions.tests: Flexibility: how you react when priorities, scope or context change, and how quickly you get back to being productive.
structure: Situation: what changed and why it was significant
Reaction: you accepted the change and clarified the new priorities
Action: you reorganised the work or learned what was needed
Result: how you delivered in the new context
Lesson
good: A positive, quick response
Concrete actions to adapt
A result achieved despite the change
pitfalls: Complaining about the change
Stories where the change was minimal
No concrete action
questions.skeleton: Midway through [a sell-side process], [the client decided to sell only one division instead of the whole company]. Most of our materials [had been built for the group]. I [asked my VP to confirm the new scope and priorities], then [rebuilt the model to separate the division's revenue, costs and shared services], and [rewrote the buyer list for the new perimeter]. Within [one week] we [relaunched the process with revised materials], and [the division attracted X bids]. I learned that [confirming the new objective first] avoids wasted work when plans change.

steps: Check that the change is significant and was not down to you.
Check that the first action is clarifying the new priorities.
Make sure the result shows a quick return to productivity.
explanation.shortcut: Change, new priorities, reorganisation, result.
explanation.trap: Focusing on how frustrating the change was: the interviewer wants to see your reaction, not your discomfort.
explanation.rule: When plans change, first clarify the new objective, then execute.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you had to learn something new very quickly.
questions.tests: Learning speed: the method you use to learn something new quickly and apply it straight away, reliably.
structure: Situation: what you had to learn, in how much time and why
Method: how you learned (sources, people, examples, practice)
Application: where you used it straight away
Result and quality check
Close with how you apply the same method today
good: An explicit, repeatable learning method
Smart use of experienced people
Practical application with a result
pitfalls: Only saying that you studied hard
No check on the quality of the work produced
Choosing something too easy
questions.skeleton: When I joined [boutique], I was staffed on [a semiconductor equipment deal] and had [one week] to understand [the industry value chain and key metrics, such as book-to-bill]. I [read the annual reports and investor presentations of the two largest peers], [wrote a one-page glossary], and [asked a sector specialist on the team for 30 minutes to test my understanding]. By [the first client call] I could [build the market section and answer the client's questions on the cycle]. I still [use the same three steps: primary sources, a summary in my own words, and a check with an expert].

steps: Check that the method is explicit and reusable.
Check that you showed a concrete, quick application.
Make sure you mentioned a quality check.
explanation.shortcut: Primary sources, personal summary, check with an expert, application.
explanation.trap: Describing hours of study instead of the method: the interviewer assesses how you learn, not how much.
explanation.rule: Learning fast means having a method, not just effort.

questions.q: Tell me about a time you had to make a decision with incomplete information.
questions.tests: Judgement under uncertainty: whether you can separate what you know from what you assume, decide in time and make your assumptions explicit.
structure: Situation: the decision, the deadline and what was missing
Action: you distinguished facts, assumptions and unknowns
Action: you chose reasonable assumptions and made them explicit (scenarios, sensitivities)
Action: you communicated the limitations and planned the update
Result and lesson
good: Stated, justified assumptions
Sensitivity or scenario analysis
A decision made in time, without waiting for perfection
pitfalls: Paralysis: waiting for data that will never arrive
Presenting assumptions as facts
Not revisiting the decision when new data arrive
questions.skeleton: For [a first-round bid analysis], we had to [give the client a view on a target's value within two days], but [the target had not yet shared its latest quarterly figures]. I [used the last audited year and the trend in listed peers' recent results to estimate current EBITDA], [built three scenarios with clear assumptions], and [flagged on the first page which numbers were estimates]. The client [submitted a range based on the base case], and when the figures arrived [our estimate was within X%]. I learned that [being explicit about assumptions] is what makes a fast decision safe.

steps: Check that you clearly separated facts and assumptions.
Check that you used scenarios or sensitivities to manage the uncertainty.
Make sure you communicated the limitations and updated the analysis with the new data.
explanation.shortcut: Facts, explicit assumptions, scenarios, communicating the limitations.
explanation.trap: Saying you waited until you had all the information: in a bank, decisions have deadlines.
explanation.rule: With incomplete data, decide, but state your assumptions and prepare scenarios.

questions.q: What energises you?
questions.tests: Which activities naturally energise you and whether they match what the role requires every day. In strengths-based interviews they also assess tone and authenticity, not just content.
structure: Answer straight away with a specific activity, not an abstract value
Explain in one sentence why it energises you
Give a recent, brief example
Link it naturally to the role, without forcing it
good: A concrete activity (e.g. solving an analytical problem, seeing a deal reach signing)
A lively, spontaneous tone
Natural alignment with an analyst's work
pitfalls: Generic answers such as 'challenges' or 'success'
Prepared, recited answers
Naming activities far removed from the role as your only source of energy
questions.skeleton: Solving a problem where [the numbers do not add up at first]. I get a real lift when [a model finally reconciles or a messy dataset starts to tell a clear story]. Last month, [on a deal, a buyer's offer looked low until I rebuilt their likely synergy case and the gap made sense]; I [stayed with it until it clicked] and enjoyed every minute. It is also why I like working on transactions: [every deal is a new puzzle with a deadline].

steps: Listen back to yourself: if the answer starts with 'I think' or a long pause, it sounds constructed. Start from the activity.
Check that the example is recent and concrete.
Check that the link to the role is natural and brief.
explanation.shortcut: Activity, why, example, link, in 45 seconds.
explanation.trap: Giving the answer you think the interviewer wants to hear: in strengths-based interviews a rehearsed tone is penalised.
explanation.rule: In strengths questions, genuine energy counts as much as content.

questions.q: When do you lose track of time?
questions.tests: The activities in which you naturally become absorbed: they are the most direct signal of your real strengths.
structure: Answer straight away with a precise activity
Describe what happens while you do it
A brief, recent example
Link it to the kind of work an analyst does
good: A specific, credible activity
Vivid details that show authenticity
Alignment with analytical or team work
pitfalls: 'When I am with friends' with no link at all
Answers that suggest poor time management
Long, reasoned-out answers
questions.skeleton: When I am [building a model from scratch or digging into a company's annual report]. I start with [one question, like why margins dropped], and two hours later I have [traced it through segments, customers and pricing]. It happened last week when [I was preparing a buyer profile and ended up mapping the company's entire supply chain]. That kind of [deep analytical work around a clear question] is what I enjoy most about my job.

steps: Check that the activity is specific, not a generic category.
Check that the details make the answer credible.
Make sure the answer stays at around 45 seconds.
explanation.shortcut: Precise activity, what happens, example, link.
explanation.trap: Answering with a hobby far removed from work and stopping there: you miss the chance to show a strength useful for the role.
explanation.rule: Whatever makes you lose track of time is a natural strength.

questions.q: Do you prefer starting tasks or finishing them?
questions.tests: Whether you can honestly pick a side and show how you compensate for the other. There is no right answer, but indecision is penalised.
structure: Pick a side straight away
Explain why in one sentence
Give a brief example
Show how you manage the less natural side (habit or method)
good: A clear, reasoned choice
Awareness of the less natural side
A concrete example
pitfalls: 'Both equally'
Choosing 'starting' and admitting that you leave things half-done
Long, theoretical answers
questions.skeleton: Finishing, honestly. I enjoy [the last mile: tying out the numbers, tightening the messages and seeing a document go out complete]. On [the last deal], I [took ownership of the final quality check of the management presentation]. Starting is less natural for me, so I [force myself to produce a quick first draft early, even if rough, to get feedback from my associate]. That way I [get the best of both]: early direction and a clean finish.

steps: Check that you picked a side in your first few words.
Check that you explained how you compensate for the less natural side.
Make sure the example is brief and real.
explanation.shortcut: One side, one reason, one example, how you compensate for the other.
explanation.trap: Saying 'both': it seems prudent but is read as a lack of self-awareness.
explanation.rule: In preference questions, pick a side and show how you manage the other.

questions.q: Are you more of a detail person or a big-picture person?
questions.tests: Self-awareness and fit with the role: an analyst must be precise on the details but understand the big picture of the deal.
structure: Pick a side straight away
An example that proves it
Show how you connect to the other side
Close by linking it to the role
good: A clear choice consistent with the role
A link between detail and the final message
A concrete example
pitfalls: Saying 'big picture' without showing attention to detail, for an analyst role
Indecision
A theoretical answer with no example
questions.skeleton: By nature I am [a detail person]: I [check every number back to its source and notice when something does not tie]. But I have learned that detail only matters if [it supports the message]. On [a recent valuation], I [found that two peers defined EBITDA differently], and the reason it mattered was [that it changed the conclusion of the page by about X turns of multiple]. So I start from the detail and always ask [what it means for the client].

steps: Check that you picked a side with an example.
Check that you showed the link between detail and the big picture.
Make sure the answer is credible for an analyst role.
explanation.shortcut: One side, one example, the bridge to the other side.
explanation.trap: Choosing 'big picture' to sound more senior: for an analyst, accuracy is the baseline requirement.
explanation.rule: For an analyst, detail is the foundation and the big picture is the direction.

questions.q: What do your friends or colleagues come to you for?
questions.tests: How others see you: an indirect way to bring out the strengths that others recognise in you.
structure: Answer with one specific thing they come to you for
Explain why you think they come to you
A recent example
Link it to how you use it at work
good: A strength recognised by others, not self-proclaimed
A concrete, recent example
Alignment with the role
pitfalls: Lists of qualities
Answers that are too personal or irrelevant
False modesty
questions.skeleton: Usually [to make sense of something complicated]: [a friend comparing two job offers, a colleague stuck on a model]. I think it is because [I ask the right questions and break problems into steps]. Last month [a colleague asked me to look at a three-statement model whose balance sheet would not balance], and we [found the issue together in twenty minutes]. At work it is the same: [I am often the person who reviews the logic before a document goes out].

steps: Check that the answer is a strength recognised by others.
Check that you gave a concrete example.
Make sure you made the link to the role.
explanation.shortcut: One thing, why, example, use at work.
explanation.trap: Listing many qualities: the question asks for one specific thing that others recognise.
explanation.rule: The most credible strengths are the ones others attribute to you.

questions.q: What kind of tasks do you find draining, or tend to put off?
questions.tests: Honesty and self-awareness: whether you admit to less natural activities and say how you manage them, without naming something central to the role.
structure: Name a real activity that is not central to the role
Explain why it drains your energy
Show how you manage it (method, order, habit)
Close with a sign that it does not affect the quality of your work
good: Credible honesty
A concrete strategy to manage it
A choice that is not critical to an analyst's work
pitfalls: Saying 'nothing'
Choosing something central (working with numbers, checking details, working late)
Complaining
questions.skeleton: Admin tasks with no clear purpose, like [expense reports or long internal forms], drain me more than complex work. I tend to [leave them for later], so I [batch them into a fixed 30-minute slot every Friday] and [use templates where I can]. That way they [never pile up or delay anything]. Interestingly, repetitive work with a clear purpose, like [updating comps], does not drain me, because [I can see what it is for].

steps: Check that the activity you chose is not central to the role.
Check that you showed a concrete method to manage it.
Make sure the tone is honest but not complaining.
explanation.shortcut: Non-central activity, why, method, no impact.
explanation.trap: Answering 'I enjoy everything': it is not credible and costs you authenticity points.
explanation.rule: Admit what drains your energy and show how you manage it.

questions.q: When are you at your best?
questions.tests: The conditions in which you perform best and whether they match the environment of a bank: pace, team, responsibility.
structure: Answer with the specific conditions
A recent example
Why those conditions help you perform
Link it to the role
good: Conditions consistent with working in a bank
A concrete example
Energy in your tone
pitfalls: Conditions far removed from the role ('when I have total freedom and no deadlines')
Vague answers
No example
questions.skeleton: I am at my best when [I own a clear piece of work, there is a real deadline and I am part of a team that depends on it]. On [a recent deal], [I was responsible for the valuation section of the board pack with three days to go], and that combination of [ownership and pace] got the best out of me. It is one reason [this role appeals to me]: [responsibility comes early, inside a strong team].

steps: Check that the conditions you describe actually exist in the role.
Check that you gave a concrete example.
Make sure your tone conveys energy.
explanation.shortcut: Conditions, example, why, link.
explanation.trap: Describing ideal conditions that banking work does not offer: it signals a possible mismatch.
explanation.rule: The conditions in which you perform best should resemble the job you are applying for.

questions.q: Do you prefer working on your own or as part of a team?
questions.tests: How you work best and whether you know that banks need both modes: focused individual work within a team.
structure: Pick a side or clearly describe your preferred balance
A concrete example
Show that you also work well in the other mode
Link it to how a deal team works
good: An honest choice with a realistic balance
A concrete example
Awareness of how a deal team works
pitfalls: 'On my own' without qualifying it, for a team role
'In a team' said in a way that sounds like dependence on others
An indecisive answer
questions.skeleton: I prefer [being part of a team, with a clear piece of work that I own]. On [deals], the best moments are [when the team comes together on the final materials], but much of my value comes from [quiet, focused hours on the model]. For example, on [a recent process], I [built the model on my own over two days, then walked the team through it and took their comments]. That mix of [individual ownership and team output] is how deal teams work.

steps: Check that you expressed a clear preference.
Check that you showed you also function well in the other mode.
Make sure the example reflects the work of a deal team.
explanation.shortcut: Preference, example, the other mode, link to the deal team.
explanation.trap: Saying 'on my own' and stopping there: for a team job it is a red flag.
explanation.rule: In banking you work on your own within a team: show both.

questions.q: How do you feel about routine or repetitive tasks?
questions.tests: Whether you have realistic expectations of an analyst's job, which includes many repetitive tasks (comps, formatting, updates), and whether you approach them with consistent quality.
structure: Answer honestly: they are not your favourite part, but you understand their value
Explain why they matter (quality of the final product, the team's trust)
Show how you make them more efficient or improve them
A brief example
good: Realism about an analyst's job
An approach focused on quality and improvement
No complaining
pitfalls: Saying 'I love repetitive tasks': hardly credible
Showing impatience
Ignoring that they are part of the role
questions.skeleton: They are not what I enjoy most, but [they are a big part of an analyst's job and where errors happen], so I take them seriously. I try to [make them faster and safer with templates, checklists and standard formulas]. At [boutique], [updating comps every week] was routine, so I [built a template that cut the time by about a third], which left more time for [the analytical work I enjoy]. Doing routine work well is [how you earn the more interesting work].

steps: Check that you showed realism: repetitive tasks are part of the role.
Check that you said how you ensure consistent quality.
Make sure you showed an initiative to improve them.
explanation.shortcut: Honesty, why they matter, how I improve them, example.
explanation.trap: Showing boredom or impatience: the interviewer worries about analysts who neglect the basic tasks.
explanation.rule: Doing routine work well is how you earn the interesting work.

questions.q: Do you prefer to follow a plan or to adapt as you go?
questions.tests: Your natural working style and whether you can balance it: M&A requires planning, but deals change constantly.
structure: Pick a side
Concrete example
How you handle the other side
Link to deal work
good: Clear preference
Awareness that deals require both
Real example
pitfalls: Indecision
Rigidity ('I always stick to the plan')
Improvisation presented as a method
questions.skeleton: I prefer [having a plan]: at the start of each deal phase I [list the deliverables, owners and deadlines]. But deals rarely follow the plan, so I treat it as [a baseline that I update]. On [a recent process], [the client changed the perimeter halfway through], and having the plan meant [I could see in ten minutes which pages were affected and re-prioritise]. So I plan carefully, and [the plan is what makes adapting fast].

steps: Check that you have picked a side.
Check that the example shows how you handle the unexpected.
Make sure you link the answer to the pace of deals.
explanation.shortcut: One side, example, how I handle the other, link to deals.
explanation.trap: Saying 'it depends' without choosing: it sounds evasive.
explanation.rule: A good plan is what makes adapting fast.

questions.q: Tell me about a deal you have followed recently.
questions.tests: Commercial awareness and analytical ability: whether you understand the strategic logic, valuation, structure and risks of a transaction, and whether you have your own view.
structure: Open with the key facts in one sentence: acquirer, target, value, multiple, form of consideration
Strategic logic: why the acquirer is buying (2 reasons)
Valuation: multiple versus comparables and precedents, premium paid
Structure and risks: financing, antitrust, integration
Close with your reasoned view and what you will watch in the coming months
good: Correct key numbers (EV, multiple, premium)
A reasoned personal view
Reference to risks and structure, not just strategy
pitfalls: Choosing a deal you know only superficially
Recounting the news without analysis
Choosing a deal you worked on and disclosing confidential information
questions.skeleton: [Acquirer] agreed to buy [target] for [an EV of X billion], about [Y times EBITDA / Z times revenue], paid in [cash / shares]. The logic is [first, access to technology or customers; second, cost synergies of about W]. The multiple looks [high / in line] against [peers at A times], which suggests [the buyer is paying away part of the synergies]. The key risks are [antitrust review in specific jurisdictions, integration and financing]. My view is that [the deal makes sense / is expensive] because [reason]. I will be watching [the regulatory decision and the next quarter's guidance].

steps: Check that you know the EV, multiple, premium and form of consideration by heart.
Check that the strategic logic has at least two concrete reasons.
Make sure you close with your own view and an argument to support it.
explanation.shortcut: Facts, logic, price, risks, view.
explanation.trap: Telling the deal as a news story without judgement: the real question is 'what do you think?'.
explanation.rule: Every deal is told through facts, logic, price, risks and a view.

questions.q: Why investment banking and not consulting?
questions.tests: Whether you understand the difference between the two jobs and whether your choice is deliberate, not random.
structure: Open by acknowledging what they have in common (problem solving, senior clients, pace)
Difference 1: in banking you work on transactions with a concrete, measurable outcome
Difference 2: valuation and financing are at the heart of the job
Personal evidence: what you enjoyed about deal work
Close with your choice
good: Respect for consulting
Concrete differences (transaction, valuation, outcome)
Personal evidence
pitfalls: Belittling consulting
Vague differences
Giving the impression that you are applying there too without conviction
questions.skeleton: Both involve [solving problems for senior clients under time pressure]. The difference for me is [the transaction]: in banking the work ends in [a deal that closes or not, with a price and a structure], while consulting often ends in [a recommendation the client may or may not implement]. I also want [valuation and financing] at the centre of what I do. At [boutique], the moment I enjoyed most was [signing day on deal], seeing months of work turn into [a binding agreement]. That is why I choose banking.

steps: Check that you acknowledged the common ground before the differences.
Check that the differences are concrete and correct.
Make sure you close with personal evidence.
explanation.shortcut: Common ground, two concrete differences, personal evidence.
explanation.trap: Calling consulting 'less concrete' dismissively: it sounds arrogant and superficial.
explanation.rule: Choose a job for its end product: in banking it is the transaction.

questions.q: Why not go straight into private equity?
questions.tests: Whether banking is a goal in itself or just a stepping stone, and whether you understand the difference between an advisor and an investor.
structure: Open with the difference between advisor and investor
Explain what banking gives you early in your career that PE does not (variety of deals, sectors, counterparties, training)
Show that you are interested in the advisory role itself
Close with your trajectory within the bank
good: Respect for and knowledge of PE work
Specific value of banking early in your career
Credible commitment to the bank
pitfalls: Admitting that banking is just a stepping stone to PE
Belittling PE
Not knowing the difference between advisor and investor
questions.skeleton: Private equity is about [investing in a few companies and owning them for years]; banking is about [advising on many transactions across sectors and counterparties]. At this stage, I value [breadth]: in one year an analyst sees [dozens of companies, several deal types and how both buyers and sellers think]. I also enjoy [the advisory role itself: running a process, working with clients and getting the deal done]. That is why I want to build my career [in investment banking, growing into a senior coverage role in technology].

steps: Check that you have explained the difference between advisor and investor correctly.
Check that the answer does not suggest banking is just a stage.
Make sure you close with a trajectory within the bank.
explanation.shortcut: Advisor versus investor, value of variety, trajectory within the bank.
explanation.trap: Saying 'PE later': for many it is true, but at a graduate interview it signals that you will leave after two years.
explanation.rule: At a bank interview, banking is the destination, not the waiting room.

questions.q: What does an analyst do day to day?
questions.tests: Whether you really know what to expect: concrete tasks, pace, responsibilities. It reduces the bank's risk of mismatched expectations.
structure: Open with the role in one sentence: the analytical and execution engine of the deal team
Task 1: models and valuations (comps, precedents, DCF, merger model)
Task 2: client materials (pitch book, information memorandum, board presentations)
Task 3: process support (data room, Q&A, coordination with lawyers and advisors)
Close with the qualities required and your experience
good: Concrete, correct tasks
Awareness of the pace and the hours
Examples from your boutique experience
pitfalls: Romanticised description ('negotiating deals with CEOs')
Complaining about the hours
List without structure
questions.skeleton: An analyst is [the analytical and execution engine of the deal team]. Day to day that means [building and updating models: trading comps, precedent transactions, DCF and merger models], [drafting client materials such as pitch books, information memoranda and board presentations], and [supporting the process: data room, buyer Q&A, coordination with lawyers and accountants]. Days are [long and driven by client deadlines]. I already do much of this at [boutique], so I know it requires [precision, speed and reliability], and I enjoy it.

steps: Check that you have cited tasks in all three areas: analysis, materials, process.
Check that the description is realistic, without emphasis on negotiations or strategic decisions.
Make sure you have linked the answer to your experience.
explanation.shortcut: Models, materials, process, qualities required.
explanation.trap: Describing the senior banker's job (negotiating, bringing in clients) instead of the analyst's.
explanation.rule: Knowing the day-to-day job is the simplest proof of motivation.

questions.q: How do you feel about the long hours?
questions.tests: Whether you have realistic expectations, whether you have already shown that you can handle intense workloads and whether you have strategies to do so sustainably.
structure: Open with realism: you know the hours are long and unpredictable
Evidence: an intense period you have already handled (at the boutique or during your studies)
Strategy: how you stay effective (planning, sleep, sport, organisation)
Close with motivation: the hours weigh less when the work interests you
good: Realism without drama
Concrete evidence of resilience
Sustainable strategies
pitfalls: 'I don't mind working 100 hours a week': not very credible
Showing excessive concern
No evidence
questions.skeleton: I know the hours are [long and often unpredictable], and I have already experienced it: at [boutique], during [a sell-side process], I worked [several weeks of late nights and weekends] to reach [signing]. What helps me is [planning the next day before I log off, protecting a few fixed things like sport when possible, and staying organised so that late nights are productive]. The hours are easier when [the work is interesting and the team is strong], which is what I expect here.

steps: Check that the answer is realistic, neither heroic nor worried.
Check that you have given concrete evidence of a workload you have already handled.
Make sure you have mentioned sustainable strategies.
explanation.shortcut: Realism, evidence, strategies, motivation.
explanation.trap: Overstating your stamina: anyone who claims to have no limits sounds naive or insincere.
explanation.rule: On hours, what counts is evidence that you have already sustained them, not a promise.

questions.q: What is your view on the M&A market right now?
questions.tests: Whether you follow the markets regularly, can link the macro context to M&A activity and have an informed view.
structure: Open with a one-sentence summary
Driver 1: rates and financing conditions
Driver 2: valuations and confidence (equity markets, the gap between the price sellers ask and the price buyers offer)
Driver 3: a sector theme (e.g. tech and semis) with a recent deal as evidence
Close with what you will watch in the coming months and your sources
good: 2-3 up-to-date, correct data points (rates, volumes, a deal)
Cause-and-effect link between macro and deal activity
Perspective on your sector
pitfalls: Old or made-up data
List of news items without a common thread
No personal view
questions.skeleton: Overall, I see [a market that is recovering / slowing]. Three drivers: first, [rates: the central bank is at X%, which sets financing costs and therefore sponsor activity]; second, [valuations: with equity markets at Y, the gap between buyers' and sellers' price expectations is narrowing / widening]; third, in [technology and semiconductors], [strategic buyers keep paying for capabilities, as in recent deal]. Over the next months I will watch [financing conditions and regulatory reviews]. I follow this through [daily financial news, deal databases and bank research].

steps: Check that every data point you cite is up to date as of the week of the interview.
Check that each driver explains its effect on M&A activity.
Make sure you close with a view and one thing to monitor.
explanation.shortcut: Summary, rates, valuations, sector, what I am watching.
explanation.trap: Reciting news without explaining the link to M&A activity.
explanation.rule: A market view is an opinion with three drivers and one data point for each.

questions.q: Pitch me an M&A idea in your sector.
questions.tests: Banker thinking: strategic logic, financial feasibility, plausible buyers or targets, risks. It is a test of disciplined creativity.
structure: Open with the idea in one sentence: who buys whom and why
Strategic logic: 2 reasons (product, customers, technology, costs)
Feasibility: relative size, financing capacity, indicative multiple
Risks: antitrust, integration, price
Close with the next step you would propose to the client
good: Plausible idea, checked against the basic numbers (relative size, leverage)
Clear strategic logic
Awareness of the risks
pitfalls: Unrealistic ideas, such as a small company buying a much larger one
Ignoring antitrust or financing constraints
Pitch without numbers
questions.skeleton: I would pitch [Acquirer, a mid-cap player in sub-segment] buying [Target, a smaller player in an adjacent segment]. The logic: [first, the target's technology fills a gap in the acquirer's roadmap; second, they share customers, so cross-selling is realistic]. It is feasible: [the target is worth about X, roughly Y% of the acquirer's market value, and the acquirer has net leverage of Z times EBITDA, so it could pay with cash and new debt]. The risks are [antitrust in specific markets and retaining engineers]. Next step: [a meeting with the acquirer's strategy team to test the idea].

steps: Check the feasibility numbers: relative size and financing capacity must be plausible (for example, a post-deal leverage that is reasonable for the sector).
Check that the strategic logic has two concrete reasons.
Make sure you have cited at least one material risk and a next step.
explanation.shortcut: Who buys whom, why, can it be paid for, risks, next step.
explanation.trap: Proposing a 'transformational' deal between two giants without considering antitrust and financing.
explanation.rule: An M&A idea is worth something if it is strategic, financeable and approvable.

questions.q: Walk me through a sell-side M&A process.
questions.tests: Whether you know the phases of a sale process and the analyst's role in each: anyone who works at a boutique must know this very well.
structure: Open with the summary: a two-round competitive auction, typically 4-6 months to signing
Preparation: mandate, analysis, materials (teaser, information memorandum, model), buyer list
First round: buyer outreach, NDA, non-binding offers
Second round: data room, management presentation, due diligence, binding offers with comments on the SPA
Close with negotiation, signing, closing and the analyst's role
good: Phases in the correct order with realistic timings
Key documents cited correctly
The analyst's role in each phase
pitfalls: Confusing binding and non-binding offers
Forgetting the NDA or the data room
Confusing signing and closing
questions.skeleton: A typical auction runs [four to six months to signing]. First, preparation: [we agree the strategy with the client, build the model, write the teaser and the information memorandum, and draft a buyer list]. Second, the first round: [we contact buyers, sign NDAs, share the memorandum and collect non-binding offers]. Third, the second round: [a shortlist gets data-room access, management presentations and due diligence, then submits binding offers with a mark-up of the SPA]. Finally, [we negotiate, sign, and close after approvals]. The analyst [runs the model, the materials and much of the process logistics].

steps: Check the order: preparation, non-binding first round, binding second round, signing, closing.
Check that you have cited the key documents: teaser, NDA, information memorandum, data room, SPA.
Make sure you have distinguished signing (signature of the contract) from closing (actual transfer after the approvals).
explanation.shortcut: Preparation, non-binding round 1, binding round 2, signing, closing.
explanation.trap: Confusing signing and closing: between the two come antitrust and regulatory approvals, which can take months.
explanation.rule: A sell-side process is a two-round auction that narrows the field and increases buyers' commitment.

questions.q: What are the main trends in your sector, and what do they mean for M&A?
questions.tests: Whether you know your sector (semis and deep tech) well enough to link industrial trends to who will buy, who will sell and at what price.
structure: Open with a one-sentence summary
Trend 1 and its implication for M&A (e.g. chip demand for AI and data centres: acquisitions of design capability and IP)
Trend 2 and its implication (e.g. industrial policy and supply-chain security: more screening of foreign investment)
Trend 3 and its implication (e.g. cyclicality in mature segments: consolidation to reach scale)
Close with your own conclusion and a recent deal as evidence
good: Concrete trends explicitly linked to M&A
Awareness of regulatory constraints, such as foreign investment screening
An example of a recent, verified deal
pitfalls: List of buzzwords without implications
Ignoring regulatory risk
Out-of-date data
questions.skeleton: Three trends stand out in [semiconductors]. First, [demand from AI and data centres] is driving [acquisitions of design capabilities and IP, often at high revenue multiples]. Second, [industrial policy and supply-chain security] mean [more deals need foreign-investment approval, which lengthens timelines and rules out some buyers]. Third, [in more mature segments, cyclicality pushes companies to consolidate to gain scale]. Together, this means [strategic buyers lead, deal certainty depends on regulators, and valuations diverge across sub-segments], as [recent deal] showed.

steps: Check that each trend has its implication for M&A.
Check that you have mentioned the regulatory factor.
Make sure you close with a recent, verified example.
explanation.shortcut: Three trends, three implications, one example.
explanation.trap: Talking about technology like an engineer rather than a banker: the question is about who buys, who sells and at what price.
explanation.rule: A sector trend matters to a banker only if it explains who will do deals and at what price.

questions.q: What is the difference between working at a boutique and at a large bank?
questions.tests: Whether you know the two business models and can explain in a balanced way why you now want the platform of a large bank.
structure: Open with the business model: pure advisory versus an integrated platform (advisory, financing, markets)
Difference 1: deal size and type, clients, international presence
Difference 2: team structure, training, specialisation
Acknowledge the advantages of the boutique (early responsibility, proximity to senior bankers)
Close with what you are looking for now
good: Balanced, correct comparison
Acknowledgement of the boutique's strengths
Link to your choice
pitfalls: Belittling the boutique
Superficial differences such as the prestige of the name
Not knowing what a large bank's balance sheet adds (capacity to finance)
questions.skeleton: A boutique offers [pure advisory, usually on mid-market deals, with small teams and very early responsibility]. A large bank combines [advisory with financing, capital markets and a global network], so it can [finance an acquisition, cover clients across regions and work on larger, more complex deals]. At [boutique] I gained [hands-on execution and close contact with senior bankers]. What I want now is [the scale, product breadth and structured training of a large platform], which is why [this programme] is the right next step.

steps: Check that the comparison is balanced and acknowledges the boutique's merits.
Check that you have cited financing capacity as a key difference.
Make sure you close with what you are looking for, not with what you are leaving.
explanation.shortcut: Business model, size, structure, the boutique's merits, what I am looking for.
explanation.trap: Reducing the difference to the prestige of the name: it sounds superficial.
explanation.rule: Compare business models, not brands.

questions.q: Explain a DCF in 60 seconds.
questions.tests: Whether you understand the logic of intrinsic valuation and can explain it in an orderly, concise way, as you would to a client.
structure: Open with the principle: a company's value is the present value of its future cash flows
Step 1: project unlevered free cash flows for 5-10 years
Step 2: calculate the terminal value (perpetuity growth or exit multiple)
Step 3: discount the cash flows and the terminal value at the WACC to get the enterprise value
Step 4: go from enterprise value to equity value by subtracting net debt; close with the sensitivity to the assumptions
good: Logical order and precise terminology (unlevered FCF, WACC, terminal value)
Remembering that the terminal value often accounts for more than half of the value
Mentioning the sensitivity to the assumptions
pitfalls: Discounting unlevered cash flows at the cost of equity
Forgetting the step from enterprise value to equity value
Going beyond 90 seconds with unnecessary detail
questions.skeleton: A DCF values a company as [the present value of its future cash flows]. First, I project [unlevered free cash flow: EBIT after tax, plus D&A, minus capex, minus the increase in working capital, for five to ten years]. Second, I estimate [a terminal value, with a perpetual growth rate or an exit multiple]. Third, I discount both at [the WACC] to get [enterprise value]. Then I subtract [net debt and other claims] to reach [equity value]. The result is very sensitive to [the WACC and the terminal assumptions], so I always show [a sensitivity table].

steps: Check consistency: unlevered cash flows are discounted at the WACC and give the enterprise value; levered cash flows are discounted at the cost of equity and give the equity value.
Check the unlevered FCF formula: EBIT × (1 - t) + D&A - capex - increase in working capital.
Make sure you have mentioned the terminal value and the sensitivity to the assumptions.
explanation.shortcut: Project, terminal value, discount at the WACC, subtract net debt.
explanation.trap: Mixing unlevered cash flows with the cost of equity: it is the most heavily penalised technical error.
explanation.rule: The discount rate must match the cash flow: unlevered with the WACC, levered with the cost of equity.

questions.q: Why is EV/EBITDA the most widely used multiple, and when would you not use it?
questions.tests: Whether you understand why a multiple is consistent (numerator and denominator relating to the same capital providers) and in which cases it is not suitable.
structure: Open with consistency: EV and EBITDA belong to all capital providers, debt and equity
Advantage 1: neutral to capital structure, so it compares companies with different leverage
Advantage 2: before D&A, so less affected by different depreciation policies
Limits: it ignores capex and working capital; not suitable for banks and insurers or for companies with negative EBITDA
Close with the alternatives: P/E, P/BV, EV/Revenue, EV/EBIT
good: Explaining the consistency between numerator and denominator
Precise limits: capital-intensive sectors, the financial sector, negative EBITDA
A correct alternative for each case
pitfalls: Saying that EBITDA is cash flow
Pairing EV with a post-interest measure, such as net income
Not being able to say when not to use it
questions.skeleton: EV/EBITDA is consistent: [enterprise value belongs to all capital providers, and EBITDA is earned before paying any of them]. So it is [unaffected by capital structure], which lets me compare [companies with different leverage], and it is [before D&A, so less distorted by different depreciation policies]. I would not rely on it for [banks and insurers, where debt is part of operations, so I use P/E or P/BV], for [companies with negative EBITDA, where I use EV/Revenue], or for [capex-heavy businesses such as chip manufacturing, where EV/EBIT or EV/(EBITDA minus capex) is better].

steps: Check consistency: with EV in the numerator you need a pre-interest measure in the denominator (EBITDA, EBIT, revenue); with equity value, a post-interest measure (net income).
Check that you have given at least two cases where the multiple does not work, with the correct alternative.
Remember capital-intensive sectors: EBITDA ignores capex, so two companies with the same EBITDA can generate very different cash.
explanation.shortcut: Same capital providers above and below the line, neutral to leverage, watch out for capex and banks.
explanation.trap: Using EV/net income or price/EBITDA: numerator and denominator relate to different capital providers.
explanation.rule: Enterprise value with pre-interest measures, equity value with post-interest measures.

questions.q: Why do companies do M&A, and what drives overall deal activity?
questions.tests: Whether you know the strategic and financial reasons for acquisitions and the market factors that push the number of deals up or down.
structure: Open with the principle: an acquisition creates value for the acquirer if the combined value exceeds the sum of the standalone values plus premium and costs
Strategic motives: growth, access to technology or markets, cost and revenue synergies, consolidation
Financial motives: deploying excess cash, tax efficiency, diversification (with caution)
Market drivers: cost and availability of debt, level and volatility of valuations, CEO confidence, regulation
Close with an example from your sector
good: Distinction between company-specific reasons and market drivers
Synergies explained with concrete examples
Reference to the cost of debt and to volatility
pitfalls: Listing motives without structure
Ignoring that many acquisitions destroy value if the acquirer overpays
Forgetting macro factors
questions.skeleton: A deal creates value for the acquirer's shareholders when [the combined business is worth more than the two standalone values plus the premium and the costs]. Companies buy for [growth they cannot achieve organically, access to technology or markets, cost synergies such as shared manufacturing, and revenue synergies such as cross-selling]. Across the market, activity is driven by [cheap and available financing, stable equity valuations, low volatility and CEO confidence], and held back by [regulation and uncertainty]. In [semiconductors], for example, [buyers often acquire IP and engineering teams to accelerate their roadmap].

steps: Check that you have separated company-specific motives from market drivers.
Check that you have explained synergies with a concrete example.
Make sure you have said when M&A creates value for the acquirer: combined value greater than the sum of the standalone values plus premium and costs.
explanation.shortcut: For the acquirer: combined value greater than the sum of the standalone values plus premium and costs; strategic motives, financial motives and market drivers.
explanation.trap: Forgetting that paying a premium larger than the synergies destroys value for the acquirer's shareholders.
explanation.rule: An acquisition creates value for the acquirer only if the synergies exceed the premium paid plus costs.

questions.q: Walk me through the three financial statements and how they link.
questions.tests: Accounting basics: whether you know how the income statement, balance sheet and cash flow statement link together, a prerequisite for any model.
structure: Income statement: from revenue to net income, over a period
Balance sheet: assets equal liabilities plus equity, at a specific point in time
Cash flow statement: from net income to the change in cash, in three sections (operating, investing, financing)
Links: net income opens the cash flow statement and flows into retained earnings; ending cash goes to the balance sheet; D&A and capex move fixed assets
Close with a quick example
good: Distinction between flow (period) and stock (point in time)
Key links named precisely
Brief example
pitfalls: Forgetting the ending cash link
Confusing profit and cash
Listing line items without explaining the links
questions.skeleton: The income statement shows [profitability over a period, from revenue down to net income]. The balance sheet shows [assets, liabilities and equity at a point in time], and it must balance. The cash flow statement [starts from net income, adds back non-cash items like D&A, adjusts for changes in working capital, then adds investing and financing flows] to get [the change in cash]. The links: [net income goes to retained earnings and starts the cash flow statement; ending cash goes to the balance sheet; capex and D&A move PP&E; debt raised or repaid moves both debt and cash].

steps: Check the main links: net income to the cash flow statement and retained earnings, ending cash to the balance sheet, capex and D&A to fixed assets.
Check that you have distinguished period (income statement, cash flow statement) from point in time (balance sheet).
Make sure you have said that the balance sheet must balance.
explanation.shortcut: IS: period; BS: point in time; CFS: bridge between profit and cash. Net income and cash are the two key links.
explanation.trap: Saying the cash flow statement starts from revenue: under the indirect method it starts from net income.
explanation.rule: Every movement in one statement must have its counterpart in the other two.

questions.q: Walk me through the three statements if depreciation increases by 10, with a 25% tax rate.
questions.tests: Whether you can follow a single change through the three statements with correct numbers: the classic first-round technical question.
structure: Income statement: EBIT -10, taxes -2.5, net income -7.5
Cash flow statement: net income -7.5, plus D&A +10 (non-cash), cash +2.5
Balance sheet, assets: fixed assets -10, cash +2.5, total -7.5
Liabilities and equity: retained earnings -7.5, total -7.5, so it balances
Close with the intuition: depreciation is not a cash outflow but it reduces taxes (tax shield)
good: Correct numbers at every step
Order: income statement, cash flow statement, balance sheet
Explanation of the tax shield
pitfalls: Saying that cash falls by 10
Forgetting the tax effect
Not checking that the balance sheet balances
questions.skeleton: On the income statement, [EBIT falls by 10; at a 25% tax rate, taxes fall by 2.5, so net income falls by 7.5]. On the cash flow statement, [net income is down 7.5, but I add back the 10 of depreciation because it is non-cash, so cash from operations rises by 2.5]. On the balance sheet, [PP&E falls by 10 and cash rises by 2.5, so assets fall by 7.5; on the other side, retained earnings fall by 7.5]. It balances. The intuition: [depreciation saves taxes of 10 times 25%, which is 2.5].

steps: Income statement: taxes fall by 10 × 0.25 = 2.5, so net income falls by 10 × (1 - 0.25) = 7.5.
Cash flow statement: -7.5 + 10 = +2.5 of cash, because depreciation is not a cash outflow.
Balance sheet: assets -10 (fixed assets) + 2.5 (cash) = -7.5; equity -7.5 (retained earnings). It balances.
explanation.shortcut: Effect on cash = increase in depreciation × tax rate = 10 × 25% = +2.5.
explanation.trap: Thinking that higher depreciation reduces cash: it reduces profit, but cash rises thanks to the tax saving.
explanation.rule: A tax-deductible non-cash expense increases cash by an amount equal to expense × tax rate.

questions.q: How do you get from enterprise value to equity value?
questions.tests: Whether you know the bridge between enterprise value and equity value and why each item is added or subtracted.
structure: Open with the definitions: EV is the value of the operating business to all capital providers; equity value is the shareholders' portion
Subtract net debt (financial debt minus cash)
Subtract other third-party claims: minorities, preferred shares, debt-like items (leases, unfunded pension obligations, depending on the convention)
Add non-operating assets excluded from EV: stakes in associates, financial investments
Close with a numerical example
good: Logic of each item explained (who has a claim on what)
Correct numerical example
Mention of debt-like items
pitfalls: Adding debt instead of subtracting it
Forgetting minorities
Confusing equity value with book equity
questions.skeleton: Enterprise value is [the value of the operating business to all capital providers]. To get to equity value, I [subtract net debt, that is debt minus cash], then [subtract other claims that rank ahead of shareholders, such as minority interests, preferred shares and debt-like items like unfunded pensions], and [add non-operating assets such as stakes in associates]. For example, [an EV of 1,000 with debt of 300, cash of 100 and minorities of 50 gives an equity value of 1,000 - 300 + 100 - 50 = 750].

steps: Start from EV and ask, for each item: who else, besides the ordinary shareholders, has a claim on this value? Those claims are subtracted.
Cash and non-operating assets belong to the shareholders but are not included in operating EV: they are added.
Example: 1,000 - 300 of debt + 100 of cash - 50 of minorities = 750 of equity value.
explanation.shortcut: Equity value = EV - net debt - minorities - preferred shares + stakes in associates.
explanation.trap: Adding debt to EV: that is the reverse bridge, from equity value to EV.
explanation.rule: From EV you subtract everything that belongs to capital providers other than the ordinary shareholders.

questions.q: When is an all-stock acquisition accretive to the acquirer's EPS?
questions.tests: Whether you know the quick accretion/dilution rule and can justify it with a numerical example.
structure: Open with the rule: in an all-stock deal it is accretive if the acquirer's P/E is higher than the P/E paid for the target, premium included
Explain why: the acquirer uses 'expensive' shares to buy earnings at a lower price
Quick numerical example
Extend to cash: it is accretive if the after-tax cost of debt is lower than the earnings yield paid (1 / P/E paid)
Close with the limit: accretive does not mean value-creating
good: Correct rule using the P/E paid, not the target's market P/E
Example with numbers that add up
Distinction between accounting accretion and value creation
pitfalls: Reversing the rule
Forgetting the premium
Saying that an accretive deal always creates value
questions.skeleton: In an all-stock deal, it is accretive if [the acquirer's P/E is higher than the P/E it pays for the target, premium included]. Intuitively, [the acquirer uses expensive shares to buy cheaper earnings]. For example, [an acquirer earning 1,000 at 20x, so worth 20,000, buys a target earning 50 for 750, which is 15x: it issues 3.75% more shares while earnings rise 5%, so EPS rises by about 1.2%]. In a cash deal, compare [the after-tax cost of debt with the earnings yield paid]. But accretion is not value creation: [it ignores whether synergies justify the premium].

steps: Acquirer: earnings 1,000, P/E 20x, market capitalisation 20,000. Target bought for 750 with 50 of earnings: P/E paid 750 / 50 = 15x.
New shares: 750 / 20,000 = 3.75% more. Combined earnings: 1,000 + 50 = 1,050, i.e. +5% (assumption: no synergies and no costs).
EPS: 1.05 / 1.0375 = 1.012, so roughly +1.2%: accretive, consistent with 20x > 15x.
explanation.shortcut: All stock: acquirer P/E > P/E paid means accretive. All cash: after-tax cost of debt < 1 / P/E paid means accretive.
explanation.trap: Using the target's market P/E and ignoring the premium: the relevant P/E is the one paid.
explanation.rule: EPS rises when you pay less for the target's earnings than the market pays for yours.

questions.q: What is WACC, and why might two companies in the same sector have different WACCs?
questions.tests: Whether you know the WACC formula and understand what drives it: operating risk, leverage, cost of debt, tax, country.
structure: Definition: the average return required by all capital providers, weighted at market values
Formula: WACC = E/(D+E) × Ke + D/(D+E) × Kd × (1 - t)
Cost of equity with the CAPM: Ke = risk-free rate + beta × equity risk premium
Why it differs: capital structure, beta, credit standing, tax rate, country and currency
Close with a sector example
good: Correct formula with the tax shield on debt
Market-value weights
Concrete reasons for the difference
pitfalls: Forgetting (1 - t) on the cost of debt
Using book-value weights
Saying that more debt always reduces the WACC, without limits
questions.skeleton: WACC is [the average return required by all capital providers, weighted by the market values of equity and debt]: [E/(D+E) times the cost of equity, plus D/(D+E) times the cost of debt times one minus the tax rate]. The cost of equity usually comes from [CAPM: the risk-free rate plus beta times the equity risk premium]. Two companies in [semiconductors] can differ because of [capital structure, different betas, for example a cyclical equipment maker versus a diversified design company, credit ratings, tax rates and the countries where they operate].

steps: Debt costs less than equity and is tax-deductible, so some leverage reduces the WACC; beyond a certain level Ke and Kd rise because of default risk.
Differences between companies in the same sector come from leverage, beta, rating, tax rate and country.
explanation.shortcut: WACC = equity weight × Ke + debt weight × Kd × (1 - t), with market-value weights.
explanation.trap: Forgetting the tax shield on debt: it overstates the WACC and understates the valuation.
explanation.rule: The WACC reflects the risk of the cash flows and the capital structure, not just the sector.

questions.q: Walk me through a basic LBO. Why does leverage increase returns?
questions.tests: Whether you understand the logic of a leveraged buyout and the three return levers: EBITDA growth, debt paydown, multiple expansion.
structure: Open with the definition: a fund buys a company, financing much of the price with debt that is repaid from the company's own cash flows
Steps: price and sources (debt and equity), projections and debt paydown, exit after 3-7 years, calculation of IRR and multiple on invested capital (MOIC)
Why leverage boosts returns: all the increase in value goes to the equity, which is a small part of the price
Numerical example
Close with the risk: more leverage means more default risk
good: The three return levers
Correct numerical example
Acknowledgement of the risk
pitfalls: Forgetting debt paydown as a source of return
Confusing IRR and MOIC
Ignoring the risk of leverage
questions.skeleton: In an LBO, [a sponsor buys a company mostly with debt, repaid from its own cash flows]. I [set the price and the debt and equity], [project cash flows and debt paydown], [assume an exit after about five years] and [compute IRR and money multiple]. Leverage boosts returns because [the whole gain goes to a smaller equity cheque]. For example, [buy for 100 with 60 of debt and 40 of equity; exit at 130 with debt down to 40; equity is worth 90, so 2.25x, versus 1.5x if the same gain of 50 sat on 100 of equity]. The cost is [higher risk if cash flows fall].

steps: Entry: price 100 = 60 of debt + 40 of equity.
Exit: value 130, remaining debt 40 (20 repaid from cash flows), equity = 130 - 40 = 90. Equity gain: 90 - 40 = 50, i.e. 30 of value increase + 20 of debt repaid.
Leveraged return: 90 / 40 = 2.25x, about 17.6% a year over 5 years (2.25^(1/5) - 1).

Without debt, the same gain of 50 (the 20 of cash would stay in the company) would sit on 100 of equity: 150 / 100 = 1.5x, about 8.4% a year. Same gain, smaller base: that is why leverage multiplies the return.
explanation.shortcut: MOIC = exit equity / entry equity; sources of return: EBITDA growth, debt paydown, multiple expansion.
explanation.trap: Calculating the return on the total price (130 / 100 = 1.3x) instead of on the equity invested (90 / 40).
explanation.rule: Leverage concentrates value creation on a smaller equity base, and the risk along with it.

questions.q: How would you value a pre-profit deep-tech company?
questions.tests: Whether you can adapt valuation methods to a company with no earnings and no track record: judgement, scenarios and triangulation, not a single formula.
structure: Open by saying that you triangulate several methods because none is enough on its own
Multiples of expected revenue or of operating metrics of listed peers and precedent transactions, adjusted for expected growth and margins
Long-term DCF (10 years or more) with scenarios, out to mature-company margins, and a discount rate that reflects the risk
Venture capital approach: future exit value discounted at a high target return, taking future dilution into account
Close with the key due diligence points: technology, intellectual property, customers, cash needs
good: Triangulation of several methods
Scenarios with explicit probabilities
Attention to cash needs and dilution
pitfalls: Applying a P/E to a loss-making company
A 5-year DCF with a terminal value that accounts for almost all of the value
Ignoring technology risk
questions.skeleton: I would triangulate. First, [EV/Revenue on forward revenue, using listed peers and recent transactions in the same niche, adjusted for growth]. Second, [a long-horizon DCF, ten years or more, with bear, base and bull scenarios until margins reach those of mature peers, weighted by probability]. Third, [a venture-style check: the expected exit value in year X discounted at a target return of Y%, adjusted for future dilution]. I would focus diligence on [technology readiness, IP, the customer pipeline and cash runway], because [they decide which scenario is realistic].

steps: Without earnings the P/E does not exist and, if EBITDA is also negative, EV/EBITDA is meaningless: you move to revenue, operating metrics or long-term cash flows.
Scenarios handle uncertainty: with probabilities of 25% bear, 50% base and 25% bull and values of 100, 300 and 800, the expected value is 0.25 × 100 + 0.5 × 300 + 0.25 × 800 = 25 + 150 + 200 = 375.
Triangulation produces a range, not a point, and due diligence decides which scenario carries the most weight.
explanation.shortcut: Revenue multiples, long scenario-based DCF, VC method: three methods, one range.
explanation.trap: Forcing a standard 5-year DCF: the terminal value accounts for almost everything and the valuation becomes arbitrary.
explanation.rule: The more uncertain the future, the more you need scenarios and triangulation.

questions.q: How many smartphones are sold in Italy each year?
questions.tests: Structured thinking under pressure: whether you break the problem down, make reasonable and stated assumptions, do clean mental arithmetic and check the result.
structure: Clarify the objective: new units sold in a year, including business phones
Break it down: population, share of users, replacement cycle
Calculate out loud with round numbers
Adjust: second-hand and refurbished phones, second work phones
Sanity check and a conclusion expressed as a range
good: Structure stated before the calculations
Round numbers and clear calculations
Final plausibility check
pitfalls: Throwing out a number without structure
Unstated assumptions
Complicated calculations that lead to errors
questions.skeleton: I would estimate it as [users divided by the replacement cycle]. Italy has [about 59 million people]; assume [about 85% own a smartphone], so [about 50 million users]. If people replace their phone [every three years on average], that gives [about 17 million phones a year]. I would adjust down for [second-hand and refurbished phones, say 10% to 15%], and up slightly for [second business phones], so [roughly 15 to 16 million]. As a sanity check, [that is about one new phone for every four people each year, which feels plausible].

steps: Users: 59 million × 85% = 50.15 million, rounded to 50 million.
Gross sales: 50 million / 3-year replacement cycle = 16.7 million, about 17 million a year.

Adjustments: 17 × (1 - 0.10) = 15.3 and 17 × (1 - 0.15) = 14.45 million, plus a small share of business phones: about 15-16 million. Check: 15.5 / 59 = 0.26, roughly one new phone for every 4 inhabitants a year.
explanation.shortcut: User base divided by the replacement cycle, then adjustments and a sanity check.
explanation.trap: Starting from shops or households without a structure: the calculations get complicated and the assumptions become invisible.
explanation.rule: In estimates, the structure and clarity of the assumptions matter more than the final number.

questions.q: What is the angle between the hour and minute hands of a clock at 3:15?
questions.tests: Reasoning under pressure and the ability not to fall for the wrong instinctive answer (zero degrees).
structure: Do not answer on instinct: reason out loud
Minute hand: 15 minutes = 90 degrees
Hour hand: 3 hours = 90 degrees, plus 15 minutes × 0.5 degrees per minute = 7.5 degrees, so 97.5 degrees
Difference: 7.5 degrees
Close with the general rule
good: Reasoning out loud
Remembering that the hour hand moves too
A general rule ready for variants
pitfalls: Answering 0 degrees on instinct
Panicking in silence
Messy calculations
questions.skeleton: Let me think it through. At [15 minutes past], the minute hand points at [the 3, which is 90 degrees from the 12]. The hour hand is not exactly on the 3: it moves [30 degrees per hour, so 0.5 degrees per minute], so after [15 minutes] it has moved [7.5 degrees past the 3, to 97.5 degrees]. The angle between them is [97.5 minus 90, which is 7.5 degrees]. In general, [the angle is the absolute value of 30 times the hour minus 5.5 times the minutes, and if it exceeds 180 you take 360 minus it].

steps: Minutes: 360° / 60 = 6° per minute; 15 × 6 = 90°.
explanation.shortcut: Angle = |30H - 5.5M|; if it exceeds 180°, take 360° minus the result.
explanation.trap: Answering 0° because both hands seem to be on the 3: the hour hand moves forward with the minutes.
explanation.rule: In brainteasers, slow down and test the assumption that seems obvious.

questions.q: Sell me this pen.
questions.tests: Commercial sense: whether you ask questions to understand the need before selling and whether you link the product to that need with confidence, through to asking for the close.
structure: Do not start by describing the pen: ask 1-2 questions about the other person's need
Link the pen to the need that emerges (signing, taking notes in meetings, making a good impression on a client)
Highlight 1-2 benefits, not features
Handle an objection
Close by explicitly asking for the sale
good: Questions before the pitch
Benefits tied to the need that emerged
Explicit close
pitfalls: Listing the pen's technical features
Talking too much without listening
Not closing
questions.skeleton: Before I tell you about it, can I ask [when you last used a pen, and what for]? [Signing a document in a client meeting.] So when it matters, [you want something reliable that looks professional in front of a client]. This pen [writes first time, every time, and looks right on the table at a signing]. You might say [you already have one]; but [is it the one you trust on the day a deal closes]? It costs [less than a coffee]. Shall I [leave it with you for your next signing]?

steps: Check that you asked at least one question before talking about the pen.
Check that you turned features into benefits tied to the need that emerged.
Make sure you closed with an explicit request.
explanation.shortcut: Question, need, benefit, objection, close.
explanation.trap: Describing the pen ('it's blue, it writes smoothly'): selling means meeting a need, not listing features.
explanation.rule: You sell what solves the client's problem, not the product itself.

questions.q: Tell me something about yourself that is not on your CV.
questions.tests: Who you are beyond the CV: authenticity, interests and personal qualities that make you pleasant to work with, even during late nights in the office.
structure: Choose an authentic, specific interest or experience
Tell one concrete detail that brings it to life
Show the quality it reveals (consistency, curiosity, team spirit)
Close with a light, not forced, link to the job
good: Authenticity and specific details
A personal quality that emerges naturally
Relaxed tone
pitfalls: Repeating something that is already on your CV
Controversial or overly personal topics
Forced links to banking
questions.skeleton: [Something specific, e.g. I have been training for and running half-marathons for four years]. What I like about it is [the routine: early mornings, a plan, and tracking small improvements week by week]. [Last spring I finally ran under X minutes after two failed attempts.] It has taught me [patience and consistency], which helps [on long deals too]. It is also [how I switch off and keep my energy up during busy periods], and I am always happy to [find running partners in a new team].

steps: Check that the topic is not already on your CV and that it is authentic.
Check that you have added a concrete detail that makes the story memorable.
Make sure any link to the job is light.
explanation.shortcut: A real interest, a detail, a quality, a light link.
explanation.trap: Forcing the link to banking ('I read financial news for fun'): it sounds contrived and takes away authenticity.
explanation.rule: This question assesses whether you are someone people work well with at two in the morning.

questions.q: Why should we not hire you?
questions.tests: Composure and self-awareness: whether you can handle a disconcerting question without tensing up, admitting a real risk as the bank sees it and showing how you manage it.
structure: Do not dismiss the question: take it seriously, calmly
Name a realistic risk from the bank's point of view (not a serious flaw)
Explain why the risk is manageable, with evidence
Close by restating your value in one sentence
good: Calm and a touch of lightness
A credible risk seen from the bank's perspective
Positive, concise close
pitfalls: Saying 'there is no reason'
Admitting a serious flaw (reliability, integrity, accuracy)
Becoming defensive
questions.skeleton: A fair concern might be [that I already have boutique experience and could find it hard to restart as a graduate and learn a new way of working]. I understand that risk. But [I chose this path deliberately because I want the breadth of a large platform], and [at boutique I have shown I adapt quickly to new teams and standards, for example when I joined a live deal halfway through the process]. So I see that experience as [a head start, not a reason to cut corners]. I am ready [to learn your way of doing things from day one].

steps: Check that you chose a realistic risk from the bank's point of view, not a serious character flaw.
Check that you showed why the risk is manageable, with evidence.
Make sure you close positively, in one sentence.
explanation.shortcut: Realistic risk, why it is manageable, evidence, positive close.
explanation.trap: Answering with a joke or with 'you should hire me': it dodges the question and signals poor self-awareness.
explanation.rule: When faced with a disconcerting question, take it seriously and bring it back to your value.
